# How to use this guide

The ER-2020 syllabus has 15 chapters. Here they are grouped into 11 units, with related chapters kept together:

| Unit | Syllabus chapters |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 Scope and terms, 2 Cell, 3 Tissues |
| 2 | 4 Osseous system and joints, 10 Skeletal muscles |
| 3 | 5 Haemopoietic system, 6 Lymphatic system |
| 4 | 7 Cardiovascular system |
| 5 | 8 Respiratory system |
| 6 | 9 Digestive system |
| 7 | 11 Nervous system |
| 8 | 12 Sense organs |
| 9 | 13 Urinary system |
| 10 | 14 Endocrine system |
| 11 | 15 Reproductive system |

Study one unit a day: read the notes, draw every labelled diagram once from memory, then answer the question bank without looking. Spend more time on the heavy chapters – blood, heart, digestion, nervous system (8 hours each in the syllabus) – and on endocrine and sense organs (6 hours each).

## Exam pattern

The D.Pharm first-year theory paper under ER-2020 is a yearly board exam of **80 marks in 3 hours** (the other 20 marks are sessional/internal). The usual ER-2020 pattern is below. Confirm the pattern with your college, since boards sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective (multiple-choice) questions – answer all | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Short answers – answer any 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| C | Long answers – answer any 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this pack:

- **MCQs** match Section A.
- **Short (3 marks)** questions match Section B – definitions, "write three functions", "what is …", "name …".
- **Long (5 marks)** questions match Section C. Some long questions cover a big topic (for example, heart structure with the conducting system); in the exam write the diagram plus the 6–8 most important points from the model answer.
- **Very-short (2 marks)** questions are quick one-line revision checks.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years or a core diagram/definition; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These are estimates from the syllabus weight and the kind of questions usually set in pharmacy diploma papers. They are not a promise.

## Scoring tips for Anatomy and Physiology

1. **Draw first.** A neat labelled diagram earns marks even before you write. Practise these until you can draw them in two minutes: cell, neuron, heart (interior), nephron, eye, ear, skin, villus, spinal cord section, reflex arc, synovial joint, long bone, female and male reproductive systems.
2. **Label with arrows and straight lines**, in pencil, on the right side of the figure. Write the title under the diagram.
3. **Learn normal values exactly**: Hb, RBC, WBC, platelets, DLC, BP 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 72/min, respiratory rate 12–20/min, GFR 125 mL/min, tidal volume 500 mL, blood glucose 70–100 mg/dL, body temperature 37 °C (98.6 °F). One correct value often gives the full MCQ mark.
4. **Use tables for comparisons**: artery vs vein, sympathetic vs parasympathetic, rods vs cones, skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth muscle, spermatogenesis vs oogenesis. Examiners mark tables quickly and kindly.
5. **Write steps as flow charts** for processes: clotting cascade, urine formation, RAAS, muscle contraction, hearing, menstrual cycle, parturition.
6. **3-mark answers:** definition + two or three points (or one small diagram). Don't write a page.
7. **5-mark answers:** heading, short definition, labelled diagram, 5–6 points, one disorder or clinical link. Six of these carry 30 marks, so practise finishing each in about 15 minutes.
8. **Link to pharmacy** in one line where you can (e.g. ACE inhibitors and RAAS, atropine and the pupil, anti-D in Rh incompatibility). It shows understanding.
9. **Spell key words correctly**: haemoglobin, oesophagus, glomerulus, parathormone, cerebellum.
10. Attempt all 20 MCQs; a blank answer is a sure zero. Read all four options before choosing – many options differ by one word (e.g. "afferent" and "efferent").

# Last-night revision sheet

## Normal values (learn exactly)

| Parameter | Normal (adult) |
| --- | --- |
| Blood volume / pH | About 5 L / 7.35–7.45 |
| Haemoglobin | Men about 13–17 g/dL; women about 12–15 g/dL |
| RBC count | Men about 4.5–5.5 million/µL; women about 4.0–5.0 million/µL |
| WBC count | 4,000–11,000/µL |
| Platelets | 1.5–4 lakh/µL |
| DLC | Neutrophils 40–75 %, lymphocytes 20–40 %, monocytes 2–10 %, eosinophils 1–6 %, basophils 0–1 % |
| RBC life | 120 days |
| BP | 120/80 mmHg; pulse pressure 40 mmHg |
| Heart rate / pulse | About 72/min (60–100) |
| Cardiac output | About 5 L/min |
| Respiratory rate | 12–20/min |
| Tidal volume / vital capacity / TLC | 500 / 4600 / 5800 mL |
| GFR / urine output | 125 mL/min (180 L/day) / about 1.5 L/day |
| Fasting blood glucose | 70–100 mg/dL |
| Body temperature | 37 °C (98.6 °F) orally |

## Unit 1 – Cell and tissues

- Anatomy = structure; physiology = function; homeostasis mostly by **negative feedback** (positive: labour, clotting).
- Mitochondria = ATP; ribosome = protein; Golgi = packing; lysosome = digestion; nucleus = control; smooth ER = lipids, detox.
- 4 tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous. Tendon = muscle–bone; ligament = bone–bone.
- Transitional epithelium = bladder; pseudostratified ciliated = trachea; stratified squamous keratinised = skin.

## Unit 2 – Bones, joints, muscle

- 206 bones (axial 80 + appendicular 126). Vertebrae 7-12-5 + sacrum + coccyx. Ribs 7 true, 3 false, 2 floating.
- Osteoblast builds, osteoclast breaks, osteocyte maintains.
- Joints: fibrous (sutures), cartilaginous (discs), synovial (free). Ball and socket = hip; hinge = knee; pivot = atlas–axis.
- Gout = urate crystals; RA = autoimmune; OA = wear.
- Contraction: ACh → Ca2+ from SR → troponin → cross-bridges → I band and H zone shorten. Myasthenia gravis = anti-ACh-receptor antibodies.

## Unit 3 – Blood and lymph

- Plasma 55 %, cells 45 %; serum = plasma − fibrinogen. Haemopoiesis in red marrow; erythropoietin from kidney.
- Clotting: prothrombin activator → thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin; Ca2+ and vitamin K (II, VII, IX, X). Haemophilia A = factor VIII.
- O universal donor, AB universal recipient; Rh − mother + Rh + baby → anti-D.
- Lymph: less protein; thoracic duct → left subclavian vein. Spleen = graveyard of RBCs (left upper abdomen).

## Unit 4 – Heart and circulation

- RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → lungs → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → body.
- SA node (pacemaker) → AV node → bundle of His → branches → Purkinje fibres.
- Cycle 0.8 s: atrial systole 0.1, ventricular systole 0.3, diastole 0.4. S1 = AV valves close, S2 = semilunar valves close.
- ECG: P atria depolarise, QRS ventricles depolarise, T ventricles repolarise; PR 0.12–0.20 s.
- BP regulation: baroreceptors (carotid sinus, aortic arch) → medulla; RAAS, ADH, adrenaline raise; ANP lowers.

## Unit 5 – Respiration

- Right lung 3 lobes, left 2. Surfactant (type II cells) prevents collapse.
- Inspiration active (diaphragm, external intercostals); quiet expiration passive.
- O2 97 % as oxyHb; CO2 70 % as HCO3− (carbonic anhydrase, chloride shift).
- Medulla = rhythm; pons = pneumotaxic/apneustic; CO2 = strongest stimulus.
- VC = TV + IRV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV; FRC = ERV + RV; IC = TV + IRV.

## Unit 6 – Digestion

- Wall: mucosa, submucosa (Meissner), muscularis (Auerbach), serosa.
- Parietal cells → HCl + intrinsic factor; chief cells → pepsinogen; G cells → gastrin.
- Villi + microvilli; lacteals absorb fat (chylomicrons); sugars and amino acids → portal blood.
- Liver: bile, glycogen, urea, plasma proteins, detoxification. Bile has no enzyme; emulsifies fat; CCK contracts gall bladder.
- Pancreatic juice alkaline: trypsin (enterokinase), amylase, lipase.

## Unit 7 – Nervous system

- CNS + PNS (12 cranial, 31 spinal pairs). Dendrite → soma → axon; myelin → saltatory conduction.
- Frontal (motor, Broca), parietal (sensory), temporal (hearing, Wernicke), occipital (vision).
- Cerebellum = balance, coordination; hypothalamus = temperature, thirst, hunger, ADH, pituitary; medulla = vital centres; basal ganglia = smooth movement (Parkinson's).
- Spinal cord ends L1–L2; dorsal root sensory, ventral root motor; reflex arc: receptor → sensory → centre → motor → effector.
- Cranial nerves: Olfactory, Optic, Oculomotor, Trochlear, Trigeminal, Abducens, Facial, Vestibulocochlear, Glossopharyngeal, Vagus, Accessory, Hypoglossal.
- Sympathetic: thoracolumbar, noradrenaline, fight or flight. Parasympathetic: craniosacral, ACh, rest and digest.

## Unit 8 – Sense organs

- Eye: sclera/cornea, choroid/ciliary body/iris, retina. Rods = dim light, rhodopsin (vit A); cones = colour, fovea. Blind spot = optic disc. Myopia → concave lens.
- Ear: pinna, canal | eardrum, malleus, incus, stapes, Eustachian tube | cochlea (organ of Corti – hearing), vestibule + semicircular canals (balance).
- Skin: epidermis (keratin, melanin), dermis (glands, receptors), vitamin D, temperature control.
- Taste: VII front two-thirds, IX back third; 5 tastes. Smell: nerve I, olfactory bulb.

## Unit 9 – Urinary system

- Nephron: glomerulus + Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct.
- Filtration (NFP ≈ 10 mmHg) → reabsorption (PCT takes all glucose) → secretion (H+, K+, drugs).
- ADH → water in collecting duct; aldosterone → Na+ in, K+ out.
- RAAS: renin → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone.
- Clearance C = UV/P; inulin = GFR; creatinine ≈ GFR; PAH = renal plasma flow.
- Micturition reflex: S2–S4, parasympathetic contracts detrusor.

## Unit 10 – Endocrine

- Anterior pituitary: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin. Posterior: ADH, oxytocin (made in hypothalamus).
- Thyroid T3/T4 (iodine, BMR) + calcitonin (lowers Ca2+). PTH raises Ca2+; lack → tetany.
- Adrenal cortex: aldosterone (salt), cortisol (sugar), androgens (sex). Medulla: adrenaline.
- Insulin (β) lowers glucose; glucagon (α) raises it. Diabetes: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia.
- Disorders: gigantism/acromegaly, diabetes insipidus, cretinism, myxoedema, Graves', goitre, Addison's, Cushing's.

## Unit 11 – Reproduction

- Testis: seminiferous tubules (sperm), Leydig cells (testosterone); epididymis stores and matures sperm.
- 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperm; 1 primary oocyte → 1 ovum + polar bodies.
- Fertilisation in ampulla of uterine tube; implantation day 6–7.
- Menstrual cycle: menses 1–5, proliferative (FSH, oestrogen), ovulation day 14 (LH surge), secretory (progesterone).
- Parturition: oxytocin positive feedback; stages – dilation, expulsion, placental.

## Diagrams to draw once tonight

Cell · neuron · heart interior · ECG · nephron · eye · ear · skin · villus · spinal cord section and reflex arc · synovial joint · long bone · male and female reproductive systems.

# Study of the compound microscope

**Aim:** To study the parts, working and care of a compound microscope.

## Principle

A compound microscope uses two lens systems. The **objective** lens forms a magnified real image of the specimen; the **eyepiece (ocular)** magnifies this image again to give an enlarged virtual image.

**Total magnification = magnification of eyepiece × magnification of objective.**

## Requirements

Compound microscope, prepared slide (e.g. blood smear), cedarwood or immersion oil, lens paper, xylene.

## Parts of the compound microscope

```text
          eyepiece (10×) ──┐
                          [ ]
             body tube ── | |
             revolving    | |      ── arm (limb)
             nosepiece ──(===)
     objectives 10×,40×,100× \|/
                stage ── ═══════════ ── stage clips
            condenser ──   (  )      ── coarse adjustment knob
    iris diaphragm ──       ‾‾       ── fine adjustment knob
     mirror / lamp ──      (O)
                base ── ▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄
```

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Base and arm | Support; hold the microscope by the arm |
| Eyepiece | Magnifies the image formed by the objective (usually 10×) |
| Body tube | Holds eyepiece and nosepiece in line |
| Revolving nosepiece | Holds and changes objectives |
| Objectives | Low power 10×, high power 40×, oil immersion 100× |
| Stage with clips | Holds the slide; mechanical stage moves it |
| Condenser | Focuses light on the specimen |
| Iris diaphragm | Controls the amount of light |
| Mirror / light source | Sends light upward (concave side for daylight) |
| Coarse and fine adjustment | Bring the specimen into focus quickly and precisely |

## Procedure

1. Place the microscope on a firm table, arm towards you; adjust the mirror for even bright light.
2. Put the slide on the stage, specimen centred over the hole; fix with clips.
3. Using the 10× objective, lower the tube with the coarse knob while watching from the side, then raise it slowly while looking through the eyepiece until the image appears.
4. Sharpen with the fine knob. Adjust the diaphragm for contrast.
5. Turn to 40× and focus with the fine knob only.
6. For 100×: place a drop of immersion oil on the slide, swing in the oil objective so it touches the oil, focus with the fine knob.
7. After use, clean the oil lens with lens paper (a trace of xylene if needed), return to low power, lower the stage and cover.

## Observations

| Eyepiece | Objective | Total magnification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10× | 10× | 100× |
| 10× | 40× | 400× |
| 10× | 100× (oil) | 1000× |

## Result

The parts of the compound microscope were identified and their functions and handling studied.

## Precautions

1. Carry with one hand under the base and one on the arm.
2. Never focus downward while looking through the eyepiece (slide may break).
3. Do not touch lenses with fingers; clean only with lens paper.
4. Use oil only with the 100× objective; wipe it off after use.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the magnification with a 10× eyepiece and 45× objective?** 450×.
2. **Why is oil used with the 100× objective?** Oil has a refractive index close to glass, so less light is lost by bending and the image is brighter and sharper.
3. **What is resolving power?** The ability to show two close points as separate.
4. **What does the iris diaphragm do?** Controls the amount of light reaching the specimen.
5. **Which knob is used at high power?** Only the fine adjustment knob.
practicals.title: Study of the compound microscope

# General techniques for the collection of blood

**Aim:** To learn the general techniques of collecting capillary and venous blood for haematological tests.

> Work only under the teacher's supervision. Use sterile disposable lancets and needles, wear gloves, and discard sharps in a puncture-proof container.

## Principle

Small volumes for Hb, cell counts, smears, blood grouping, BT and CT are taken by **skin puncture** (capillary blood) from the fingertip, ear lobe or (in infants) the heel. Larger volumes are taken by **venepuncture** from a superficial vein, usually the median cubital vein at the elbow. An **anticoagulant** is added when unclotted blood is needed.

| Anticoagulant | How it works | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EDTA (dipotassium salt) | Binds calcium | Blood counts, smears |
| Trisodium citrate 3.8 % | Binds calcium | ESR (1:4), coagulation tests (1:9) |
| Double oxalate | Precipitates calcium | Some counts, PCV |
| Heparin | Inhibits thrombin (with antithrombin) | Some chemistry tests |

## Requirements

Sterile lancet, 70 % alcohol (spirit) swabs, dry cotton, gloves; for venepuncture – tourniquet, sterile syringe and needle (or vacuum tube), anticoagulant tubes, labels, sharps container.

## Procedure A: Capillary blood (finger prick)

1. Choose the side of the tip of the ring or middle finger; warm and massage the hand to improve flow.
2. Clean with spirit and **let it dry** (wet spirit causes haemolysis and stings).
3. Hold the finger firmly and make a quick prick 2–3 mm deep with the lancet.
4. **Wipe away the first drop** (it contains tissue fluid).
5. Let a free-flowing drop form without squeezing hard; collect as required.
6. Press with dry cotton to stop bleeding.

## Procedure B: Venous blood (venepuncture)

1. Seat the subject with the arm extended; tie the tourniquet 7–8 cm above the elbow (not more than about one minute).
2. Ask the subject to make a fist; feel for the median cubital vein.
3. Clean the site with spirit and let it dry.
4. Insert the needle bevel up at about 15–30° along the vein; draw blood slowly.
5. Release the tourniquet, then withdraw the needle and press with cotton.
6. Transfer blood gently into labelled tubes and mix with the anticoagulant by gentle inversion (do not shake).

## Observations

| Site | Volume collected | Container | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fingertip | Few drops | Slide / pipette | Hb, counts, grouping |
| Median cubital vein | ___ mL | EDTA / citrate tube | ESR, counts |

## Result

Capillary and venous blood were collected by the correct aseptic technique.

## Precautions

1. Strict asepsis; never reuse lancets or needles.
2. Allow spirit to dry before pricking.
3. Avoid squeezing the finger (dilutes blood with tissue fluid).
4. Label every sample with name, date and time.
5. Do not leave the tourniquet on too long.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the first drop wiped off?** It is mixed with tissue fluid and gives wrong values.
2. **Which vein is preferred for venepuncture?** Median cubital vein – large, superficial, well fixed.
3. **Which anticoagulant is used for ESR?** 3.8 % trisodium citrate.
4. **Why does EDTA prevent clotting?** It binds calcium, which is needed for clotting.
5. **Name sites for skin puncture.** Fingertip, ear lobe, heel (infants).
practicals.title: General techniques for the collection of blood

# Microscopic examination of tissues (permanent slides)

**Aim:** To study epithelial tissue, cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, skeletal muscle, connective tissue and nervous tissue under the microscope using pre-prepared slides.

## Principle

Thin stained sections show the shape, arrangement and special features of the cells of each tissue. Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and eosin stains cytoplasm and fibres pink (H and E stain).

## Requirements

Compound microscope, permanent slides of the tissues, immersion oil, lens paper, record book and pencil.

## Procedure

1. Focus each slide first under low power (10×) to see the general pattern.
2. Change to high power (40×) to see cell details.
3. Draw a labelled diagram in pencil and note identifying features.

## Observations

| Slide | Identifying features | Location / function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Simple squamous epithelium** | Single layer of flat cells with central flat nuclei, like floor tiles | Alveoli, blood vessels; diffusion |
| **Simple cuboidal epithelium** | Single layer of square cells with round central nuclei | Kidney tubules, glands; secretion |
| **Simple columnar epithelium** | Tall cells, oval nuclei at the base, goblet cells | Stomach, intestine; absorption |
| **Stratified squamous epithelium** | Many layers; basal cells cuboidal, surface cells flat | Skin, oesophagus; protection |
| **Skeletal muscle** (longitudinal section) | Long unbranched fibres, cross-striations, many peripheral nuclei | Attached to bones; voluntary |
| **Cardiac muscle** | Branched striated fibres, one central nucleus, dark intercalated discs | Heart; involuntary |
| **Smooth muscle** | Spindle-shaped cells, one central nucleus, no striations | Gut, vessels; involuntary |
| **Areolar connective tissue** | Loose network of pink collagen and thin elastic fibres with scattered cells | Under the skin; binds organs |
| **Hyaline cartilage** | Glassy matrix, chondrocytes in lacunae, often in pairs | Trachea, joint surfaces |
| **Compact bone (transverse section)** | Haversian systems – central canal, concentric lamellae, lacunae with canaliculi | Skeleton |
| **Nervous tissue (neurons)** | Large multipolar cell bodies with processes; nucleus with prominent nucleolus | Brain, spinal cord |

```text
  Skeletal (L.S.)          Cardiac                 Smooth
 |o||||||||||||o|      ==<‖==o==/‖==            __/o\__  __/o\__
 |  o||||||||||||      ==‖==o===‖==           /_______\/_______\
  striated,            branched, central       spindle, no stripes
  peripheral nuclei    nucleus, discs ‖        one central nucleus
```

## Result

The given slides were identified as ______ on the basis of the features recorded above.

## Precautions

1. Begin with low power before high power.
2. Handle slides by the edges; do not break cover slips.
3. Draw exactly what is seen; label with straight lines.

## Viva questions

1. **How do you identify cardiac muscle?** Branched striated fibres with central nuclei and intercalated discs.
2. **What are goblet cells?** Mucus-secreting cells in columnar epithelium.
3. **What is a Haversian system?** The unit of compact bone – central canal with rings of lamellae and osteocytes.
4. **Which epithelium lines the alveoli?** Simple squamous.
5. **What does eosin stain?** Cytoplasm and fibres pink.

# Study of the human skeleton (axial and appendicular)

**Aim:** To study the bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton using an articulated skeleton and loose bones.

## Principle

The adult skeleton has 206 bones: the **axial skeleton** (80 bones – skull, ear ossicles, hyoid, vertebral column, thoracic cage) forms the central axis, and the **appendicular skeleton** (126 bones – girdles and limbs) is attached to it.

## Requirements

Articulated human skeleton (model), loose bones (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, humerus, femur, hip bone etc.), charts.

## Procedure

1. Identify each bone on the articulated skeleton and note its position.
2. Pick up the loose bone, hold it in the anatomical position and identify the side (right or left) from its features.
3. Note important features, joints formed and muscles or structures related.
4. Draw neat labelled sketches.

## Observations

**Axial skeleton (80)**

| Part | Bones | Number | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Skull – cranium | Frontal, parietal (2), temporal (2), occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid | 8 | Sutures; foramen magnum in occipital |
| Skull – face | Nasal, maxilla, zygomatic, lacrimal, palatine, inferior conchae (2 each), vomer, mandible | 14 | Mandible the only movable skull bone |
| Ear ossicles | Malleus, incus, stapes (each side) | 6 | Stapes smallest bone |
| Hyoid | U-shaped | 1 | No joint with other bones |
| Vertebral column | Cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacrum, coccyx | 26 | Atlas, axis; bodies largest in lumbar region |
| Thoracic cage | Sternum 1, ribs 24 | 25 | True 7, false 3, floating 2 pairs |

**Appendicular skeleton (126)**

| Part | Bones (each side) |
| --- | --- |
| Pectoral girdle | Clavicle, scapula |
| Upper limb | Humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges |
| Pelvic girdle | Hip bone (ilium + ischium + pubis; acetabulum) |
| Lower limb | Femur, patella, tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges |

**Identifying features (examples):** humerus – round head fits glenoid cavity of scapula; femur – head fits acetabulum, longest bone; tibia – sharp anterior border (shin), medial malleolus; typical thoracic vertebra – facets for ribs, long downward spine.

## Result

The bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton were identified and their features studied.

## Precautions

1. Handle bones and models gently.
2. Hold a bone in the anatomical position before deciding its side.

## Viva questions

1. **How many bones in the axial and appendicular skeleton?** 80 and 126.
2. **Which is the only movable bone of the skull?** Mandible.
3. **Which bones form the hip bone?** Ilium, ischium and pubis.
4. **Name the first two cervical vertebrae.** Atlas (C1) and axis (C2).
5. **Which is the largest sesamoid bone?** Patella.
practicals.title: Study of the human skeleton (axial and appendicular)

# Determination of blood group

**Aim:** To determine the ABO and Rh blood group of the given blood sample (slide method).

## Principle

Blood groups depend on antigens (agglutinogens) on the RBC surface. When RBCs carrying an antigen meet the matching antibody (antisera), they clump together – **agglutination**.

- Anti-A serum clumps RBCs with antigen A; anti-B clumps antigen B; anti-D clumps Rh (D)-positive cells.

## Requirements

Clean glass slide (or tile), antisera anti-A (blue), anti-B (yellow) and anti-D, sterile lancet, spirit swabs, cotton, toothpicks or mixing sticks, glass marker.

## Procedure

1. Mark three areas on a clean slide: A, B and D.
2. Place one drop of anti-A, anti-B and anti-D serum in the marked areas.
3. Clean the fingertip with spirit, let it dry, prick and discard the first drop.
4. Add one small drop of blood near each antiserum drop.
5. Mix each with a separate clean stick, spreading into a circle.
6. Rock the slide gently for about 1–2 minutes (anti-D up to about 3 minutes) and look for clumping with the naked eye (or a hand lens) against a white background.

## Observations

| Anti-A | Anti-B | Anti-D | Blood group |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| + | − | + | A positive |
| − | + | + | B positive |
| + | + | + | AB positive |
| − | − | + | O positive |
| (as above) | (as above) | − | Same ABO group, Rh negative |

(+ = agglutination, − = no agglutination)

Your sample: Anti-A ___, Anti-B ___, Anti-D ___.

## Result

The blood group of the given sample is ______ (Rh ______).

## Precautions

1. Use a separate stick for each drop so sera are not mixed.
2. Blood drop should be smaller than the serum drop.
3. Read within the time given; drying at the edges can look like clumping.
4. Check expiry date of antisera.

## Viva questions

1. **Who discovered the ABO system?** Karl Landsteiner.
2. **Which group is the universal donor and universal recipient?** O is the universal donor; AB is the universal recipient.
3. **What is agglutination?** Clumping of RBCs when antigen meets its antibody.
4. **Why is Rh group important in pregnancy?** An Rh-negative mother may form anti-D against an Rh-positive baby, causing haemolytic disease of the newborn in a later pregnancy.
5. **Is a cross-match still needed before transfusion?** Yes, to check compatibility of donor cells with recipient serum.
practicals.title: Determination of blood group

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of ESR (Westergren method)

**Aim:** To determine the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of the given blood sample by the Westergren method.

## Principle

When anticoagulated blood stands in a vertical tube, RBCs settle down under gravity, leaving clear plasma above. The fall of the upper level of RBCs in **one hour**, measured in mm, is the ESR. Stacking of RBCs (rouleaux), favoured by raised fibrinogen and globulins in inflammation, makes them settle faster.

## Requirements

Westergren tube (200 mm long, graduated 0–200 mm), Westergren stand, 3.8 % trisodium citrate, syringe and needle, test tube, timer.

## Procedure

1. Take 0.4 mL of 3.8 % trisodium citrate in a clean tube.
2. Collect venous blood and add 1.6 mL to the citrate (ratio 4 parts blood : 1 part citrate). Mix gently by inversion.
3. Draw the mixture into the Westergren tube exactly to the 0 mark, avoiding air bubbles.
4. Fix the tube **exactly vertical** in the stand at room temperature, away from vibration and sunlight.
5. Start the timer. After exactly **1 hour**, read the height of the clear plasma column from 0 to the top of the RBC column.

## Observations

| Time | Reading (mm) |
| --- | --- |
| Start | 0 |
| After 1 hour | ___ |

## Normal values (Westergren, approx.)

- Men: 0–15 mm in the first hour
- Women: 0–20 mm in the first hour (slightly higher; also higher in pregnancy and old age)

**ESR rises in:** tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis, rheumatic fever, infections, anaemia, multiple myeloma, pregnancy. **ESR falls in:** polycythaemia, sickle-cell anaemia. ESR is a non-specific test – it shows that disease is present, not which one.

## Result

The ESR of the given sample is ___ mm in the first hour (Westergren method), which is ______ (normal / raised).

## Precautions

1. Keep the blood–citrate ratio exactly 4:1.
2. Tube must be clean, dry and exactly vertical (a tilt speeds up settling).
3. Avoid air bubbles and clotting.
4. Do the test within about 2 hours of collection; read at exactly 60 minutes.

## Viva questions

1. **Define ESR.** The distance in mm that RBCs fall in anticoagulated blood in a vertical tube in one hour.
2. **Which anticoagulant and ratio are used?** 3.8 % trisodium citrate, 1 part to 4 parts blood.
3. **Name another method.** Wintrobe method.
4. **Why does ESR rise in inflammation?** More fibrinogen and globulins promote rouleaux formation.
5. **Is ESR diagnostic?** No – it is non-specific; useful to follow disease activity (e.g. TB, RA).
practicals.title: Determination of ESR (Westergren method)

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of haemoglobin content (Sahli's method)

**Aim:** To estimate the haemoglobin content of the given blood sample by Sahli's acid haematin method.

## Principle

Haemoglobin is converted to brown **acid haematin** by 0.1 N HCl. The brown solution is diluted with distilled water until its colour matches the standard brown glass rods of the comparator. The Hb value (g/dL) is read directly from the graduated tube.

Hb + 0.1 N HCl → acid haematin (brown)

## Requirements

Sahli's haemoglobinometer (comparator with standard brown glass, graduated tube, Hb pipette marked 20 µL (20 cu mm), stirrer, dropper), 0.1 N HCl, distilled water, lancet, spirit, cotton.

## Procedure

1. Fill the graduated tube with 0.1 N HCl up to the lowest mark (mark 2 g% or the "20" mark as given on your tube).
2. Prick the finger; discard the first drop.
3. Suck blood exactly to the 20 µL mark of the Hb pipette; wipe the outside of the tip.
4. Blow the blood into the bottom of the acid; rinse the pipette with the acid by sucking up and blowing out 2–3 times; mix with the stirrer.
5. Allow to stand for **10 minutes** for full conversion to acid haematin.
6. Add distilled water drop by drop, stirring after each addition, and compare with the standard against daylight.
7. Stop when the colour exactly matches. Read the lower level of the meniscus in g/dL (g%).

## Observations

| Trial | Reading (g/dL) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | ___ |
| 2 | ___ |
| Mean | ___ |

**Normal haemoglobin (approx.):** men 13–17 g/dL; women 12–15 g/dL; newborn higher (about 14–20 g/dL).

Low Hb = **anaemia** (iron deficiency, blood loss, B12/folate deficiency); high Hb = polycythaemia, dehydration, high altitude.

## Result

The haemoglobin content of the given blood sample is ___ g/dL, which is ______.

## Precautions

1. Fill the pipette exactly to the mark without air bubbles; wipe the outside.
2. Wait the full 10 minutes before diluting.
3. Add water slowly – once over-diluted, the test must be repeated.
4. Match colour in daylight, with the tube in the comparator.

## Viva questions

1. **What is formed when blood is mixed with 0.1 N HCl?** Brown acid haematin.
2. **Why wait 10 minutes?** For complete conversion of Hb to acid haematin.
3. **What is the main error of Sahli's method?** Colour matching by eye is subjective, and some Hb forms (e.g. carboxyhaemoglobin) are not converted.
4. **Name a more accurate method.** Cyanmethaemoglobin (Drabkin) method.
5. **Normal Hb in adult males?** About 13–17 g/dL.
practicals.title: Determination of haemoglobin content (Sahli's method)

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of bleeding time and clotting time

**Aim:** To determine the bleeding time (Duke's method) and clotting time (capillary tube method) of the given subject.

## Principle

- **Bleeding time (BT):** the time from a standard skin puncture until bleeding stops. It depends mainly on **platelet** number and function and on capillary constriction.
- **Clotting time (CT):** the time from the escape of blood until it forms a clot (fibrin threads appear). It depends on the **clotting factors** (coagulation cascade).

## Requirements

Sterile lancet, spirit swabs, cotton, filter paper (circular), stopwatch, glass capillary tubes (about 10 cm long, 1–2 mm bore).

## Procedure A: Bleeding time (Duke's method)

1. Clean the fingertip (or ear lobe) with spirit and let it dry.
2. Make a quick puncture about 3 mm deep and **start the stopwatch** as the first drop appears.
3. Do not squeeze. Every **30 seconds**, touch the drop gently with the edge of the filter paper without touching the skin.
4. Move to a fresh part of the paper each time. The spots become smaller.
5. **Stop the watch** when no more blood stains the paper.
6. BT = number of blood spots × 30 seconds (or the time on the watch).

## Procedure B: Clotting time (capillary tube method)

1. Prick the finger and **start the stopwatch** when blood appears.
2. Fill a capillary tube with the free-flowing blood (hold it slightly downward).
3. After 2 minutes, break off a small piece of the tube every **30 seconds**, gently separating the pieces.
4. Note the time when a **fibrin thread** is first seen between the broken pieces. This is the clotting time.

## Observations

| Test | Spots / breaks | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bleeding time | ___ spots × 30 s | ___ min |
| Clotting time | Thread seen at break no. ___ | ___ min |

**Commonly quoted normal ranges** (vary with method; use your lab manual's range): BT about 1–5 minutes (Duke); CT about 4–10 minutes (capillary tube).

- **BT prolonged:** thrombocytopenia (e.g. dengue), platelet function defects, aspirin use, von Willebrand disease.
- **CT prolonged:** haemophilia, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, anticoagulant therapy (heparin). In haemophilia **BT is normal but CT is prolonged**.

## Result

Bleeding time = ___ minutes; clotting time = ___ minutes. Both are ______ (within / outside the normal range).

## Precautions

1. Do not squeeze the finger or touch the wound with the filter paper.
2. Start timing at the first appearance of blood.
3. Use clean, dry capillary tubes; break pieces gently.
4. Room temperature affects CT – do the test at normal room temperature.

## Viva questions

1. **What does bleeding time test?** Platelet function and vessel constriction.
2. **What does clotting time test?** The coagulation factors.
3. **In haemophilia, which is prolonged?** Clotting time; bleeding time stays normal.
4. **Why does aspirin prolong BT?** It blocks thromboxane A2 formation in platelets.
5. **What is the fibrin thread?** Insoluble fibrin formed from fibrinogen by thrombin.
practicals.title: Determination of bleeding time and clotting time

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of total WBC count

**Aim:** To determine the total leucocyte (WBC) count of the given blood sample using a haemocytometer.

## Principle

Blood is diluted 20 times with **Turk's fluid**, which lyses the RBCs (glacial acetic acid) and stains WBC nuclei (gentian violet). The WBCs are counted in a known volume of the **Neubauer counting chamber**, and the count per mm³ (per µL) of blood is calculated.

## Requirements

Haemocytometer (improved Neubauer chamber, WBC pipette with white bead marked 0.5, 1 and 11, cover slip), Turk's fluid (about 2 % glacial acetic acid tinted with gentian violet), microscope, lancet, spirit, cotton.

## The Neubauer chamber

```text
   Ruled area 3 mm × 3 mm = 9 large squares (each 1 mm²)

   ┌─────┬─────┬─────┐
   │ W   │     │  W  │   W = four corner squares used for WBC
   │     │     │     │       (each divided into 16 smaller squares)
   ├─────┼─────┼─────┤
   │     │  R  │     │   R = central square (25 groups) for RBC
   ├─────┼─────┼─────┤
   │ W   │     │  W  │   Depth (cover slip to floor) = 0.1 mm
   └─────┴─────┴─────┘
```

## Procedure

1. Clean the chamber and cover slip; place the cover slip over the ruled area.
2. Prick the finger, discard the first drop; draw blood to the **0.5 mark** of the WBC pipette. Wipe the tip.
3. Draw Turk's fluid up to the **11 mark** (dilution 1 in 20). Mix by rolling the pipette for 2–3 minutes.
4. Discard the first few drops (fluid in the stem has no cells).
5. Touch the tip to the edge of the cover slip and let the chamber fill by capillary action, without overflow or bubbles.
6. Wait 2–3 minutes for cells to settle. Count WBCs under low power in the **four corner large squares**. Count cells touching the top and left lines, not those on the bottom and right lines.

## Observations and calculation

| Square | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | Total (N) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WBCs | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |

- Area counted = 4 × 1 mm² = 4 mm²; depth = 0.1 mm; volume = 0.4 mm³.
- Dilution = 20.

**Total WBC/mm³ = (N × dilution) ÷ volume = (N × 20) ÷ 0.4 = N × 50**

**Worked example:** N = 150 → 150 × 50 = **7,500 cells/mm³** (normal).

**Normal:** 4,000–11,000/mm³. More = leucocytosis (bacterial infection, leukaemia); less = leucopenia (typhoid, some viral infections, drug toxicity).

## Result

The total WBC count of the given sample is ______ cells/mm³, which is ______.

## Precautions

1. Fill the pipette exactly to the marks; no air bubbles.
2. Mix well and discard the first drops.
3. Do not overfill the chamber.
4. Follow the "count top and left, not bottom and right" rule to avoid counting a cell twice.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the composition of Turk's fluid?** Glacial acetic acid (lyses RBCs) and gentian violet (stains nuclei) in water.
2. **What is the dilution in WBC counting?** 1 in 20.
3. **Why discard the first drops from the pipette?** The stem holds diluting fluid without cells.
4. **What is the multiplication factor?** 50.
5. **Why is the bead in the pipette bulb?** It helps mixing and identifies the pipette.
practicals.title: Determination of total WBC count

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of total RBC count

**Aim:** To determine the total red blood cell count of the given blood sample using a haemocytometer.

## Principle

Blood is diluted 200 times with **Hayem's fluid** (isotonic; preserves RBCs and keeps them separate). RBCs are counted in a known small volume of the Neubauer chamber and the number per mm³ of blood is calculated.

## Requirements

Haemocytometer (improved Neubauer chamber, RBC pipette with red bead marked 0.5, 1 and 101, cover slip), Hayem's fluid (sodium chloride, sodium sulphate and mercuric chloride in water) or another isotonic RBC diluent, microscope, lancet, spirit, cotton.

## Procedure

1. Place the clean cover slip on the chamber.
2. Prick the finger, discard the first drop; draw blood exactly to the **0.5 mark** of the RBC pipette. Wipe the tip.
3. Draw Hayem's fluid up to the **101 mark** (dilution 1 in 200). Mix by rolling for 2–3 minutes.
4. Discard the first few drops; charge the chamber by capillary action.
5. Wait 2–3 minutes. Under high power (40×), count RBCs in **5 medium squares** of the central large square – the four corners and the centre one (each has 16 smallest squares, 80 smallest squares in all).

```text
   Central 1 mm² square = 25 medium squares (each 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm)
   ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
   │ 1 │   │   │   │ 2 │   Count squares 1–5
   ├───┼───┼───┼───┼───┤   (each = 16 tiny squares)
   │   │   │   │   │   │
   ├───┼───┼───┼───┼───┤
   │   │   │ 5 │   │   │
   ├───┼───┼───┼───┼───┤
   │   │   │   │   │   │
   ├───┼───┼───┼───┼───┤
   │ 3 │   │   │   │ 4 │
   └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
```

## Observations and calculation

| Square | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | Total (N) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RBCs | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |

- Area of 5 medium squares = 5 × (1/25) mm² = 1/5 mm²; depth 0.1 mm; volume = 1/50 mm³ (0.02 mm³).
- Dilution = 200.

**RBC/mm³ = (N × 200) ÷ 0.02 = N × 10,000**

**Worked example:** N = 480 → 480 × 10,000 = **4.8 million/mm³** (normal).

**Normal:** men about 4.5–5.5 million/mm³; women about 4.0–5.0 million/mm³. Low = anaemia; high = polycythaemia (high altitude, dehydration).

## Result

The total RBC count of the given blood sample is ______ million/mm³, which is ______.

## Precautions

1. Fill exactly to the marks; mix well.
2. Count under high power; distribute cells evenly (no clumps).
3. Use the "top and left lines counted" rule.
4. Clean the pipette with water, alcohol and ether after use.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the dilution in RBC counting?** 1 in 200.
2. **Why is Hayem's fluid used?** It is isotonic, so RBCs neither swell nor shrink, and it prevents clumping.
3. **What is the multiplication factor?** 10,000.
4. **Why is the RBC count higher in people living at high altitude?** Low O2 stimulates erythropoietin and more RBCs are made.
5. **What colour is the bead in the RBC pipette?** Red.

# Determination of differential leucocyte count (DLC)

**Aim:** To prepare and stain a blood smear and determine the percentage of each type of white blood cell.

## Principle

A thin blood film is stained with **Leishman's stain** (a Romanowsky stain: eosin + methylene blue in methyl alcohol). Methyl alcohol fixes the cells; nuclei stain purple-blue, eosinophil granules orange-red, basophil granules dark blue. **100 WBCs** are counted and classified, so each count equals a percentage.

## Requirements

Clean grease-free slides, spreader slide, Leishman's stain, buffered (or distilled) water, dropper, staining rack, microscope with oil immersion, cedarwood/immersion oil, lancet, spirit, cotton.

## Procedure

**A. Preparing the smear**

1. Put a small drop of blood about 1–2 cm from one end of a clean slide.
2. Hold the spreader at about 45°, touch the drop, let blood spread along its edge, and push forward in one smooth movement.
3. A good smear is thin, tongue-shaped, with a feathered tail. Air-dry it.

**B. Staining**

4. Cover the smear with Leishman's stain (count the drops); leave 2 minutes (fixation).
5. Add double the number of drops of buffered water; mix by blowing gently; leave 7–10 minutes (staining).
6. Wash with water, wipe the back, air-dry.

**C. Counting**

7. Examine under oil immersion, in the thin part near the tail, moving in a zig-zag (battlement) path.
8. Identify and tally 100 WBCs.

```text
   Neutrophil      Eosinophil      Basophil       Lymphocyte     Monocyte
    (o(o)o)         ( o o )        (#####)          (  O  )       (   C   )
   3–5 lobed,      2 lobes,        dark blue      large round    largest,
   fine pink-      orange-red      granules       nucleus, thin  kidney-shaped
   violet granules granules        hide nucleus   blue rim       nucleus
```

## Observations

| Cell | Tally | Number (%) | Normal range (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neutrophils | | ___ | 40–75 |
| Lymphocytes | | ___ | 20–40 |
| Monocytes | | ___ | 2–10 |
| Eosinophils | | ___ | 1–6 |
| Basophils | | ___ | 0–1 |
| **Total** | | **100** | |

**Clinical meaning:** neutrophilia – bacterial infection; lymphocytosis – viral infections, TB; eosinophilia – allergy, asthma, worm infestation; monocytosis – TB, malaria.

## Result

The differential leucocyte count is: N ___ %, L ___ %, M ___ %, E ___ %, B ___ %.

## Precautions

1. Slides must be grease-free; smear must be thin and even.
2. Do not let the stain dry on the slide.
3. Count in the thin area and avoid counting the same field twice.

## Viva questions

1. **What does Leishman's stain contain?** Eosin and methylene blue dissolved in methyl alcohol.
2. **Why is methyl alcohol present?** It fixes the cells to the slide.
3. **Which WBC is most common?** Neutrophils.
4. **Which cell rises in allergy?** Eosinophil.
5. **Why count 100 cells?** So the number of each type equals its percentage directly.

# Recording of blood pressure in different postures, arms and after exertion

**Aim:** To record the arterial blood pressure of a human subject by the auscultatory method in different postures, in both arms, and before and after exercise, and to interpret the results.

## Principle

A cuff on the arm is inflated to stop flow in the brachial artery and then slowly deflated. When cuff pressure falls just below systolic pressure, blood spurts through the narrowed artery and makes tapping sounds (**Korotkoff sounds**) heard by a stethoscope.

- **Systolic pressure** = pressure at the first clear tapping sound (phase 1).
- **Diastolic pressure** = pressure when the sounds disappear (phase 5).

## Requirements

Sphygmomanometer (mercury, aneroid or digital) with a cuff of correct size, stethoscope, couch, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Let the subject rest for 5 minutes. Seat them with the arm supported at heart level, palm up.
2. Wrap the deflated cuff snugly round the upper arm, its lower edge 2–3 cm above the elbow crease.
3. **Palpatory method first:** feel the radial pulse, inflate until it disappears, note this value (approximate systolic), deflate.
4. **Auscultatory method:** place the stethoscope over the brachial artery at the elbow. Inflate to about 30 mmHg above the palpatory value.
5. Deflate slowly (2–3 mmHg per second). Note the first tapping sound (systolic) and the point where sounds disappear (diastolic).
6. Deflate fully; wait 1–2 minutes before repeating.
7. Repeat in: (a) **lying** (supine), (b) **sitting**, (c) **standing** (record immediately and after 2 minutes); (d) the **other arm**; (e) **immediately after exercise** (e.g. 2 minutes of spot jogging or stair climbing) and again after 5 minutes rest.

## Observations

| Condition | Arm | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) | Pulse pressure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lying | Right | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Sitting | Right | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Standing | Right | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Sitting | Left | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| After exercise | Right | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| After 5 min rest | Right | ___ | ___ | ___ |

**Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic; mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure.**
Example: 120/80 mmHg → pulse pressure 40, MAP ≈ 93 mmHg.

## Interpretation

- Normal adult: about 120/80 mmHg; persistent readings of 140/90 mmHg or more suggest hypertension.
- **Standing:** blood pools in the legs; baroreceptor reflex keeps BP nearly steady (diastolic may rise slightly). A fall of 20 mmHg systolic or more on standing = **orthostatic (postural) hypotension**.
- **Two arms:** a small difference (usually under about 10 mmHg) is normal.
- **After exercise:** systolic rises (higher cardiac output) while diastolic changes little or falls (vasodilation in muscles); values return to normal within a few minutes of rest.

## Result

The BP of the subject at rest (sitting) is ___/___ mmHg. Changes with posture, arm and exercise are recorded above and are ______.

## Precautions

1. Correct cuff size; cuff at heart level.
2. Do not deflate too fast; avoid prolonged inflation (pain, error).
3. Subject should be relaxed, not talking, no smoking or caffeine just before.

## Viva questions

1. **What are Korotkoff sounds?** Sounds from turbulent flow in a partly compressed artery, heard during deflation of the cuff.
2. **Why is the palpatory method done first?** To avoid missing an auscultatory gap and to know how high to inflate.
3. **What is pulse pressure?** Systolic minus diastolic pressure, normally about 40 mmHg.
4. **Why does systolic BP rise after exercise?** Heart rate and stroke volume increase.
5. **What is postural hypotension?** A fall in BP on standing, causing dizziness.

# Recording of body temperature, pulse rate and respiratory rate

**Aim:** To record body temperature with mercury, digital and infrared thermometers at different sites, the pulse/heart rate at different sites before and after exertion, and the respiratory rate of a human subject.

## Principle

Temperature, pulse, respiration and BP are the **vital signs**. Body temperature is kept near 37 °C by the hypothalamus; it varies slightly with the site of measurement. The **pulse** is the rhythmic expansion of an artery with each heartbeat, so the pulse rate normally equals the heart rate. Respiratory rate is the number of breaths per minute.

## Requirements

Clinical mercury thermometer (handle carefully – mercury is toxic; many labs now use digital ones), digital thermometer, infrared (forehead/ear) thermometer, spirit swabs, watch with a seconds hand, stethoscope.

## Procedure A: Body temperature

1. **Mercury (oral):** clean the bulb with spirit, shake the mercury below 35 °C, place under the tongue with lips closed for 2–3 minutes, read at eye level.
2. **Axillary:** dry the armpit, keep the bulb in the axilla with the arm pressed to the side for about 5 minutes (mercury) or until the digital beep.
3. **Digital:** switch on, place orally or in the axilla, read after the beep.
4. **Infrared:** aim at the forehead (or in the ear canal for a tympanic model) as per instructions; read instantly.
5. The subject should not eat, drink hot/cold liquids or smoke for 15 minutes before an oral reading.

## Procedure B: Pulse rate

1. Seat the subject relaxed. Place the tips of index, middle and ring fingers on the **radial artery** at the wrist (thumb side).
2. Count for a full minute; note rate, rhythm (regular/irregular) and volume.
3. Repeat at other sites: carotid (neck – press one side only, gently), brachial (elbow), femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis.
4. Compare with the **apex beat** (heart rate) counted with a stethoscope at the 5th left intercostal space.
5. Ask the subject to exercise (spot jogging 2 minutes); count the pulse immediately and every minute until it returns to resting.

## Procedure C: Respiratory rate

1. Without telling the subject (breathing changes when noticed), watch or feel the rise and fall of the chest/abdomen while appearing to count the pulse.
2. Count for one full minute; note rhythm and depth.

## Observations

| Thermometer / site | Reading |
| --- | --- |
| Mercury – oral | ___ °C |
| Mercury – axillary | ___ °C |
| Digital – oral | ___ °C |
| Infrared – forehead | ___ °C |

| Pulse site | Rest (/min) | After exercise (/min) | After 5 min rest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Radial | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Carotid | ___ | ___ | ___ |

Respiratory rate: ___ /min.

## Normal values (adult, approx.)

- Oral temperature about 37 °C (98.6 °F), range about 36.5–37.5 °C; axillary reading is usually about 0.5 °C lower and rectal about 0.5 °C higher than oral. Fever = above about 37.5–38 °C.
- Pulse 60–100/min (average 72); above 100 = tachycardia, below 60 = bradycardia (normal in trained athletes).
- Respiratory rate 12–20/min.
- After exercise, pulse and respiration rise and return to resting levels within a few minutes in a fit person.

## Result

Temperature, pulse and respiratory rate were recorded as above and are ______ (normal / abnormal).

## Precautions

1. Clean thermometers between users; handle mercury thermometers carefully (spill = toxic).
2. Do not use the thumb to feel the pulse (it has its own pulse).
3. Do not press both carotids together.
4. Count respiration without the subject noticing.

## Viva questions

1. **Which part of the brain controls body temperature?** Hypothalamus.
2. **Why is the thumb not used to feel the pulse?** Its own pulse can be confused with the subject's.
3. **What is pulse deficit?** Difference between heart rate (apex) and pulse rate, as in atrial fibrillation.
4. **Why does the pulse rate rise after exercise?** Sympathetic activity and adrenaline raise the heart rate to supply more O2 to muscles.
5. **Normal respiratory rate in adults?** 12–20 breaths per minute.
practicals.title: Recording of body temperature, pulse rate and respiratory rate

# Recording of pulse oxygen saturation (before and after exertion)

**Aim:** To record the oxygen saturation of arterial blood (SpO2) and pulse rate with a pulse oximeter before and after exertion.

## Principle

A pulse oximeter clips on a fingertip. It shines **red and infrared light** through the finger. Oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin absorb these two lights differently. By measuring absorption only during the pulsatile (arterial) part of each beat, the device calculates the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen – **SpO2** – and also shows the pulse rate.

## Requirements

Fingertip pulse oximeter, spirit swabs, nail-polish remover if needed, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Seat the subject and let them rest for 5 minutes. Hands should be warm.
2. Remove nail polish or artificial nails from the test finger (usually the index or middle finger).
3. Switch on the oximeter and place the finger fully inside, nail upward. Keep the hand still and at heart level.
4. Wait until the reading is steady (about 30–60 seconds) and a good pulse waveform/bar appears. Record SpO2 and pulse rate.
5. Ask the subject to exercise (e.g. 2–3 minutes of stair climbing or spot jogging).
6. Record SpO2 and pulse immediately after exercise and then every minute for 5 minutes.

## Observations

| Time | SpO2 (%) | Pulse rate (/min) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rest | ___ | ___ |
| Immediately after exercise | ___ | ___ |
| 1 min | ___ | ___ |
| 3 min | ___ | ___ |
| 5 min | ___ | ___ |

## Interpretation

- **Normal SpO2 at rest: about 95–100 %** in healthy people at sea level.
- Readings persistently below about 94 % need attention; around 90 % or less indicates significant **hypoxaemia** (e.g. pneumonia, COPD, severe asthma).
- In a healthy subject SpO2 stays nearly the same after moderate exercise while the pulse rises; a clear fall in SpO2 on exertion suggests heart or lung disease.

## Result

Resting SpO2 = ___ %, pulse ___ /min; after exertion SpO2 = ___ %, pulse ___ /min. The values are ______.

## Precautions

1. Cold fingers, poor circulation, movement, bright light and nail polish give false readings.
2. Wait for a steady reading with a good signal.
3. The oximeter cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning.

## Viva questions

1. **What does SpO2 mean?** Percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen measured by a pulse oximeter.
2. **What lights are used?** Red and infrared.
3. **Normal SpO2?** About 95–100 %.
4. **Why does nail polish affect the reading?** It absorbs and blocks the light.
5. **Name one clinical use.** Monitoring patients with pneumonia, COVID-19, asthma, during anaesthesia.
practicals.title: Recording of pulse oxygen saturation (before and after exertion)

# Recording of peak expiratory flow with a peak flow meter

**Aim:** To record the force of air expelled from the lungs – the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) – using a peak flow meter.

## Principle

**Peak expiratory flow rate** is the maximum speed of air (litres per minute) blown out in a short, sharp forced expiration after a full inspiration. It depends mainly on the diameter of the large airways and the strength of the expiratory muscles. It falls when the airways are narrowed, as in **asthma** and COPD, so it is used to monitor these patients at home.

## Requirements

Mini Wright (or similar) peak flow meter with a disposable mouthpiece, predicted PEFR chart (by age, sex and height), height scale.

## Procedure

1. Note the subject's age, sex and height.
2. Fix a clean mouthpiece; move the pointer to zero.
3. The subject **stands** (or sits upright), holds the meter horizontally without blocking the scale or the vent with the fingers.
4. Take the **deepest possible breath**, close the lips tightly round the mouthpiece, and blow out **as hard and fast as possible** in one short blast (a "huff" – not a slow long breath).
5. Read the pointer position (L/min); return it to zero.
6. Repeat **three times** with rest in between. Record the **highest** of the three.
7. Compare with the predicted value from the chart.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | PEFR (L/min) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | ___ |
| 2 | ___ |
| 3 | ___ |
| Best | ___ |

Predicted PEFR (from chart) = ___ L/min

**Percentage of predicted = (best reading ÷ predicted) × 100**

Example: best 400 L/min, predicted 500 L/min → 80 % of predicted.

## Interpretation (zone system used in asthma care)

| Zone | % of predicted / personal best | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green | 80–100 % | Good control |
| Yellow | 50–80 % | Caution – airways narrowing; follow action plan |
| Red | Below 50 % | Medical alert – urgent treatment |

PEFR is higher in men, taller people and young adults; lower in women, children and the elderly. A rise after a bronchodilator inhaler shows reversible airway narrowing (asthma).

## Result

The best PEFR of the subject = ___ L/min, which is ___ % of the predicted value (______ zone).

## Precautions

1. Correct posture and a tight seal round the mouthpiece.
2. Blow short and sharp; do not cough or spit into the meter.
3. Use a fresh mouthpiece for each person.
4. Take the best of three, not the average.

## Viva questions

1. **Define PEFR.** Maximum rate of air flow during a forced expiration after full inspiration.
2. **Unit of PEFR?** Litres per minute.
3. **In which disease is it most useful?** Bronchial asthma.
4. **Why is the best of three taken?** Effort varies; the best reading shows true capacity.
5. **How does a bronchodilator change PEFR in asthma?** It increases it by widening the airways.
practicals.title: Recording of peak expiratory flow with a peak flow meter

# Measurement of height, weight and BMI

**Aim:** To measure the height and weight of a subject and calculate the body mass index (BMI).

## Principle

**Body mass index** relates weight to height and is used to screen for underweight, overweight and obesity.

**BMI = weight (kg) ÷ [height (m)]²** (unit kg/m²)

## Requirements

Stadiometer or wall-mounted height scale with a head-board, weighing machine (calibrated, set to zero), calculator.

## Procedure

**Height**

1. Subject removes shoes and headwear, stands straight on a flat floor with heels together, back of heels, buttocks, shoulders and back of head touching the scale.
2. Head held level (looking straight ahead).
3. Lower the head-board gently to touch the top of the head; read to the nearest 0.5 cm. Convert to metres.

**Weight**

4. Check the machine reads zero.
5. Subject in light clothing, without shoes, stands still in the centre of the platform.
6. Read to the nearest 0.1 kg (or 0.5 kg).

## Observations and calculation

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Height | ___ cm = ___ m |
| Weight | ___ kg |
| BMI | ___ kg/m² |

**Worked example:** weight 68 kg, height 1.65 m → BMI = 68 ÷ (1.65 × 1.65) = 68 ÷ 2.72 ≈ **25.0 kg/m²**.

## Interpretation

| BMI (kg/m²) | WHO classification (adults) |
| --- | --- |
| Below 18.5 | Underweight |
| 18.5–24.9 | Normal |
| 25.0–29.9 | Overweight |
| 30 and above | Obese |

For Asian Indians, lower cut-offs are often used because health risk starts at lower BMI: normal about 18.5–22.9, overweight 23–24.9, obese 25 and above. By these, the worked example above would be classed as obese, though it is at the WHO overweight border.

**Limitations:** BMI does not separate muscle from fat (athletes may read "overweight"), and does not show where fat is stored; waist circumference adds this information. Not used in the same way for children (age-specific charts) or pregnant women.

## Result

Height ___ m, weight ___ kg, BMI ___ kg/m², which falls in the ______ category.

## Precautions

1. Remove shoes and heavy clothing.
2. Zero the weighing machine before use.
3. Keep the head level when measuring height.
4. Measure at the same time of day when comparing readings.

## Viva questions

1. **Formula of BMI?** Weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²).
2. **Normal BMI range (WHO)?** 18.5–24.9 kg/m².
3. **Why are lower cut-offs used for Indians?** Diabetes and heart-disease risk rises at lower BMI in South Asians.
4. **One limitation of BMI?** It cannot tell fat from muscle.
5. **Why is BMI important for pharmacists?** Obesity counselling and some drug doses are based on body weight.
practicals.title: Measurement of height, weight and BMI

# Study of organ systems with charts, models and specimens

**Aim:** To study the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urinary, endocrine, reproductive and nervous systems, and the eye, ear and skin, with the help of charts, models and specimens.

## Principle

Models and charts show the shape, position and internal structure of organs that cannot be seen in a living person. Identifying the parts and linking each to its function builds the base for theory answers and viva.

## Requirements

Torso model, heart, lung, kidney, brain, eye, ear and skin models; charts of each system; preserved specimens where available.

## Procedure

1. Identify the system and the position of each organ on the torso model or chart.
2. Open the model (where possible) and name the internal parts.
3. Write the function of each part.
4. Draw a neat labelled diagram in the record.

## Observations

| System / organ | Parts to identify | Key functions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cardiovascular (heart model)** | Four chambers, tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic valves, chordae tendineae, aorta, venae cavae, pulmonary trunk and veins, coronary arteries | Pumping of blood; pulmonary and systemic circulation |
| **Respiratory** | Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea with rings, bronchi, lungs (3 right lobes, 2 left), pleura, diaphragm | Air conduction and gas exchange |
| **Digestive** | Mouth, oesophagus, stomach (fundus, body, pylorus), duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, colon, rectum, liver, gall bladder, pancreas | Digestion and absorption |
| **Urinary (kidney model)** | Cortex, medulla, pyramids, calyces, pelvis, ureter, bladder, urethra; nephron chart | Urine formation, fluid and salt balance |
| **Endocrine** | Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreas (islets), ovaries/testes | Hormone secretion |
| **Reproductive** | Male: testes, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, urethra. Female: ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina | Gamete and hormone production; pregnancy |
| **Nervous (brain model)** | Cerebral lobes, cerebellum, midbrain, pons, medulla, spinal cord, cranial nerves | Control and coordination |
| **Eye** | Cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary body, retina, optic nerve, aqueous and vitreous humour | Vision |
| **Ear** | Pinna, external canal, tympanic membrane, malleus, incus, stapes, Eustachian tube, cochlea, semicircular canals | Hearing and balance |
| **Skin** | Epidermis layers, dermis, hair follicle, sebaceous and sweat glands, receptors, hypodermis | Protection, temperature control, sensation |

## Result

The organ systems were studied with models, charts and specimens and their parts identified and labelled.

## Precautions

1. Handle models carefully; replace parts in the right position.
2. Draw diagrams in pencil and label on one side with straight lines.

## Viva questions

1. **Which chamber of the heart has the thickest wall?** Left ventricle.
2. **How many lobes does each lung have?** Right 3, left 2.
3. **Which gland is called the master gland?** Pituitary.
4. **Name the three ear ossicles.** Malleus, incus, stapes.
5. **Where is the nephron's glomerulus located – cortex or medulla?** Cortex.
6. **Which part of the eye controls pupil size?** Iris.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
2. Diagram: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus with nucleolus and chromatin, mitochondria, rough and smooth ER, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, centrioles.
3. Cell membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins (fluid mosaic model); selectively permeable; transport, receptors, cell recognition.
4. Nucleus: double membrane with pores; contains DNA (chromatin); controls cell activities, heredity; nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
5. Mitochondria: double membrane, cristae; aerobic respiration and ATP production (power house).
6. Ribosomes: protein synthesis. Rough ER: makes and transports proteins. Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis, drug detoxification, Ca2+ store in muscle.
7. Golgi apparatus: modifies, packs and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes.
8. Lysosomes: digestive enzymes; destroy worn-out parts and bacteria (suicide bags).

questions.answer:
1. Tissue = group of similar cells doing a common function. Four types: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous.
2. Characteristics of epithelium: closely packed cells, little matrix, rests on basement membrane, avascular, regenerates well.
3. Simple squamous – alveoli, blood vessel lining, Bowman's capsule – diffusion and filtration.
4. Simple cuboidal – kidney tubules, thyroid follicles – secretion and absorption.
5. Simple columnar – stomach and intestine (goblet cells, microvilli) – absorption and secretion.
6. Ciliated columnar – uterine tubes; pseudostratified ciliated columnar – trachea – moves mucus.
7. Stratified squamous keratinised – skin; non-keratinised – mouth, oesophagus, vagina – protection.
8. Transitional – urinary bladder, ureter – stretching.
9. Glandular epithelium – exocrine (with ducts) and endocrine (ductless) glands.
10. Draw simple squamous, cuboidal and columnar epithelium.
questions.question: Classify tissues of the human body. Describe epithelial tissue with its types, locations and functions.

questions.answer: Largest organelle, usually central. Double nuclear membrane with pores (lets RNA out). Nucleoplasm contains chromatin (DNA + protein) that forms 46 chromosomes in division. Nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and ribosomes. Functions: controls all cell activities and metabolism, stores genetic information, DNA replication before division, RNA synthesis for protein production. RBCs lack a nucleus; skeletal muscle fibres have many.
questions.question: Write a note on the nucleus.

questions.answer: Homeostasis: keeping the internal environment (temperature, glucose, pH, BP, water) nearly constant. Control system: receptor → control centre → effector. Negative feedback reverses the change – rise in blood glucose → insulin → glucose falls; rise in temperature → sweating, vasodilation → cooling. Most body controls work this way. Positive feedback increases the change until an event ends it – oxytocin in labour, blood clotting, LH surge. Failure of homeostasis causes disease (diabetes, hypertension).

questions.answer: Passive (no ATP): simple diffusion of O2, CO2 and lipid-soluble drugs from high to low concentration; facilitated diffusion with carrier or channel (glucose); osmosis of water through the membrane. questions.answer: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body and its parts. Physiology is the study of the functions of the body and its parts. Example: the thin wall of the alveolus (anatomy) suits gas exchange (physiology).

2. Classification: fibrous/immovable (skull sutures), cartilaginous/slightly movable (intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis), synovial/freely movable.
