# Unit 7: Nervous system

Syllabus chapter 11: classification of the nervous system; anatomy and physiology of the cerebrum, cerebellum and midbrain; functions of the hypothalamus, medulla oblongata and basal ganglia; spinal cord – structure and reflexes; names and functions of cranial nerves; anatomy and physiology of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems (ANS).

The nervous system senses changes inside and outside the body, decides what to do, and controls muscles and glands. It works fast, by electrical impulses and chemical transmitters.

## 7.1 Classification of the nervous system

```text
                       NERVOUS SYSTEM
            _________________|__________________
           |                                    |
   CENTRAL (CNS)                       PERIPHERAL (PNS)
   - Brain                             - 12 pairs cranial nerves
   - Spinal cord                       - 31 pairs spinal nerves
                               ______________|_______________
                              |                              |
                     Afferent (sensory)            Efferent (motor)
                     receptors → CNS                CNS → effectors
                                          ____________|____________
                                         |                         |
                                  Somatic (voluntary)    AUTONOMIC (involuntary)
                                  → skeletal muscle      → heart, smooth muscle,
                                                           glands
                                                      _______|_______
                                                     |               |
                                               Sympathetic    Parasympathetic
```

## 7.2 Neuron – the structural and functional unit

```text
                       NEURON (motor, myelinated)

  dendrites                                    myelin sheath
    \  |  /                                    (Schwann cell)    node of
     \ | /          axon hillock               _____   _____    Ranvier
  ----( • )====>==================[_____]=[_____]=[_____]=====< axon
       cell                  |                                 terminals
       body               AXON (carries impulse away          (synaptic
      (nucleus,            from the cell body)                 knobs)
      Nissl bodies)
   Direction of impulse:  dendrites → cell body → axon → terminals
```

- **Cell body (soma)** – nucleus, Nissl granules (rough ER), neurofibrils.
- **Dendrites** – short, branched; carry impulses **towards** the cell body.
- **Axon** – single long process; carries impulses **away** from the cell body. Many axons have a **myelin sheath** (fatty insulation) with gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**; impulses jump from node to node (**saltatory conduction**), so myelinated fibres conduct faster.
- **Types by function:** sensory (afferent), motor (efferent), interneurons (association, in CNS).
- **Types by structure:** multipolar (motor), bipolar (retina), unipolar/pseudounipolar (sensory ganglia).
- **Neuroglia** support neurons (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells, Schwann cells).

**Nerve impulse (brief):** resting membrane potential about −70 mV (Na+ outside, K+ inside, kept by the Na+/K+ pump). A stimulus opens Na+ channels → Na+ rushes in → **depolarisation** (action potential) → K+ moves out → **repolarisation**. It follows the all-or-none law.

**Synapse:** junction between two neurons. The impulse releases a **neurotransmitter** (acetylcholine, noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, GABA, glutamate) from the presynaptic knob; it crosses the synaptic cleft and acts on receptors of the next cell. Transmission is one-way.

## 7.3 Protection of the CNS

- **Bones:** skull and vertebral column.
- **Meninges** (three membranes): **dura mater** (outer, tough), **arachnoid mater** (middle, web-like), **pia mater** (inner, delicate, on the brain surface). The subarachnoid space (between arachnoid and pia) contains **CSF**. Inflammation = meningitis.
- **Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF):** clear fluid (about 120–150 mL) made by the **choroid plexuses** in the four **ventricles** of the brain; cushions the brain, carries nutrients and removes wastes; absorbed into venous sinuses via arachnoid villi. Sample taken by **lumbar puncture**.
- **Blood–brain barrier:** tight capillary walls that keep many drugs and toxins out of the brain.

## 7.4 Parts of the brain

```text
          BRAIN (side view, simplified)

              ________ CEREBRUM ________
             /  frontal  | parietal     \
            |   lobe     |  lobe         |
            |____________|_____ occipital|
             \ temporal lobe     \ lobe  /
              \__________________ \____/
                  | DIENCEPHALON  |  ___________
                  | (thalamus,    | | CEREBELLUM|
                  |  hypothalamus)| |___________|
                  | MIDBRAIN      |
                  | PONS          |   BRAINSTEM =
                  | MEDULLA       |   midbrain + pons + medulla
                  |_______________|
                        | spinal cord
```

The adult brain weighs about 1.3–1.4 kg.

### Cerebrum

- Largest part; two **cerebral hemispheres** joined by the **corpus callosum**.
- Outer **cerebral cortex** of **grey matter** (cell bodies), folded into **gyri** (ridges) and **sulci** (grooves); inner **white matter** (myelinated tracts) with deep grey masses (basal ganglia).
- Each hemisphere controls the **opposite side** of the body (fibres cross over).

| Lobe | Main functions |
| --- | --- |
| **Frontal** | **Primary motor area** (precentral gyrus – voluntary movement); **Broca's (motor speech) area** (usually left side); thinking, judgement, personality, planning |
| **Parietal** | **Primary somatosensory area** (postcentral gyrus – touch, pain, temperature, position); understanding of sensations |
| **Temporal** | **Hearing** (auditory area); **Wernicke's area** (understanding speech); memory; smell |
| **Occipital** | **Vision** (visual area) |

**Functions of the cerebrum:** intelligence, learning, memory, reasoning, speech, voluntary movement, conscious sensation, emotion.

### Diencephalon

- **Thalamus** – relay station for almost all sensory impulses (except smell) to the cortex; crude awareness of pain.
- **Hypothalamus** – small but very important (below the thalamus, connected to the pituitary).

**Functions of the hypothalamus**

1. **Controls the autonomic nervous system** (heart rate, BP, gut activity).
2. **Body temperature regulation** ("thermostat").
3. **Hunger and satiety** (feeding centres) and **thirst**.
4. **Water balance** – makes **ADH**; also **oxytocin** (stored in the posterior pituitary).
5. **Controls the anterior pituitary** through releasing and inhibiting hormones – link between the nervous and endocrine systems.
6. Sleep–wake cycle and circadian rhythm.
7. Emotions and behaviour (with the limbic system) – fear, rage, pleasure; sexual behaviour.

### Midbrain

- Upper part of the brainstem, between the diencephalon and pons. Contains the **cerebral aqueduct**, cerebral peduncles (tracts), and the **corpora quadrigemina**: superior colliculi (**visual reflexes** – turning eyes towards light or movement) and inferior colliculi (**auditory reflexes** – turning head towards sound).
- Contains the **substantia nigra** (dopamine-producing; its loss causes Parkinson's disease) and nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV.
- **Functions:** relay pathway between cerebrum and lower parts; visual and auditory reflexes; control of eye movements and pupil size; posture.

### Pons

- Bridge of fibres between the cerebellum, medulla and higher centres; has the **pneumotaxic and apneustic** respiratory centres; nuclei of cranial nerves V–VIII.

### Medulla oblongata

- Lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord. Motor tracts **cross over** (decussation of pyramids) here.

**Functions of the medulla oblongata (vital centres)**

1. **Cardiac centre** – controls heart rate and force.
2. **Vasomotor centre** – controls the diameter of blood vessels and so BP.
3. **Respiratory centre** – sets the rhythm of breathing.
4. **Reflex centres** – swallowing, vomiting, coughing, sneezing, hiccupping, salivation.
5. Carries all tracts between the brain and spinal cord; nuclei of cranial nerves IX–XII.

Damage to the medulla is often fatal because of these vital centres.

### Cerebellum

- Second largest part; behind the brainstem, below the occipital lobe. Two hemispheres joined by the vermis; outer grey cortex, inner white matter ("arbor vitae").
- **Functions:** coordination of voluntary movements (smooth, accurate movement); **maintains balance and equilibrium** (with the inner ear); **muscle tone and posture**; motor learning of skilled movements.
- Damage → **ataxia** (unsteady gait), intention tremor, poor balance.

### Basal ganglia (basal nuclei)

- Masses of grey matter deep in the cerebrum: caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus (with links to the substantia nigra and subthalamic nucleus).
- **Functions:** control and smoothing of voluntary movement, starting and stopping movements, regulation of muscle tone, control of automatic movements such as arm swinging while walking.
- Disorders: **Parkinson's disease** (dopamine deficiency – tremor, rigidity, slow movement), Huntington's chorea.

## 7.5 Spinal cord – structure and reflexes

**Structure**

- Cylindrical cord about **45 cm** long, from the foramen magnum (continuous with the medulla) to the level of the **first–second lumbar vertebra**, within the vertebral canal. Below this the nerve roots form the **cauda equina**.
- Two enlargements: cervical (nerves to arms) and lumbar (nerves to legs).
- **31 pairs of spinal nerves:** cervical 8, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 5, coccygeal 1.
- Each spinal nerve is formed by a **dorsal (posterior) root** (sensory; has a **dorsal root ganglion**) and a **ventral (anterior) root** (motor); so spinal nerves are **mixed** nerves.

```text
        Spinal cord – cross section

              posterior median sulcus
          dorsal root   |   dorsal root ganglion (•)
            (sensory) \ | /
         ______________\|/______________
        /  WHITE MATTER (tracts)        \
       |      \  posterior horn  /       |
       |       \    (sensory)   /        |
       |        \____ __ ______/  GREY   |
       |         |   (o)   |   MATTER    |  (o) = central canal (CSF)
       |        /    lateral \  (H or    |
       |       /  anterior horn\ butterfly)
        \_____/___(motor)_______\_______/
               /        \
     ventral root (motor)   anterior median fissure
```

- **Grey matter** (inside, H-shaped): posterior horns (sensory), anterior horns (motor neurons), lateral horns (autonomic, in thoracic region).
- **White matter** (outside): **ascending (sensory) tracts** carry impulses up to the brain (e.g. spinothalamic – pain and temperature); **descending (motor) tracts** carry impulses down (e.g. corticospinal/pyramidal – voluntary movement).

**Functions:** conducts impulses between body and brain; centre for **spinal reflexes**.

**Reflex action** – a fast, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, without conscious thought. The pathway is a **reflex arc**:

```text
   REFLEX ARC (e.g. withdrawal from a hot object)

  1. RECEPTOR (skin) ──→ 2. SENSORY NEURON ──→ (dorsal root)
                                                    │
                              3. INTEGRATING CENTRE (spinal cord grey matter,
                                 often via an interneuron)
                                                    │
  5. EFFECTOR (muscle) ←── 4. MOTOR NEURON ←── (ventral root)
        contracts → hand pulled away
```

**Examples:** knee jerk (patellar reflex – a **monosynaptic stretch reflex**, tests spinal segments L2–L4), withdrawal reflex, plantar reflex, blinking, coughing, sneezing (cranial reflexes). Doctors test reflexes to check the nervous system.

## 7.6 Cranial nerves (12 pairs)

| No. | Name | Type | Main function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | **Olfactory** | Sensory | Smell |
| II | **Optic** | Sensory | Vision |
| III | **Oculomotor** | Motor | Most eye movements, raising the eyelid, pupil constriction, focusing |
| IV | **Trochlear** | Motor | Eye movement (superior oblique muscle) |
| V | **Trigeminal** | Mixed | Sensation of face, scalp, teeth; muscles of chewing |
| VI | **Abducens** | Motor | Eye movement outward (lateral rectus) |
| VII | **Facial** | Mixed | Muscles of facial expression; taste (front two-thirds of tongue); tears and saliva |
| VIII | **Vestibulocochlear (auditory)** | Sensory | Hearing (cochlear part) and balance (vestibular part) |
| IX | **Glossopharyngeal** | Mixed | Taste (back third of tongue); swallowing; parotid saliva; carotid body/sinus impulses |
| X | **Vagus** | Mixed | Parasympathetic supply to heart, lungs and gut; swallowing; voice (larynx) |
| XI | **Accessory** | Motor | Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (head and shoulder movement) |
| XII | **Hypoglossal** | Motor | Tongue movements |

**Mnemonic for names:** "**O**h **O**h **O**h **T**o **T**ouch **A**nd **F**eel **V**ery **G**ood **V**elvet **A**h **H**eaven."
**Mnemonic for type (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both):** "**S**ome **S**ay **M**arry **M**oney, **B**ut **M**y **B**rother **S**ays **B**ig **B**rains **M**atter **M**ore."

## 7.7 Autonomic nervous system (ANS)

The ANS controls involuntary organs – heart, smooth muscle (gut, blood vessels, bronchi, bladder, eye) and glands – mainly through the hypothalamus and brainstem. Each pathway has **two neurons**: a **preganglionic** neuron (from CNS to a ganglion) and a **postganglionic** neuron (from ganglion to the organ).

| Feature | **Sympathetic** | **Parasympathetic** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin (outflow) | **Thoracolumbar** (T1–L2 segments of the spinal cord) | **Craniosacral** (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2–S4) |
| Ganglia | Close to the spinal cord (**sympathetic chain**) | Close to or in the wall of the organ |
| Preganglionic fibre | Short | Long |
| Postganglionic fibre | Long | Short |
| Transmitter at ganglion | Acetylcholine | Acetylcholine |
| Transmitter at organ | **Noradrenaline** (adrenergic) – except sweat glands (ACh) | **Acetylcholine** (cholinergic) |
| Overall role | **"Fight or flight"** – prepares body for stress and exercise | **"Rest and digest"** – conserves energy |

**Effects on organs**

| Organ | Sympathetic | Parasympathetic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eye (pupil) | Dilates (mydriasis) | Constricts (miosis) |
| Heart | Rate and force increase | Rate decreases |
| Bronchi | Dilate | Constrict |
| Blood vessels (skin, gut) | Constrict | — (little effect) |
| Salivary glands | Little, thick saliva | Much watery saliva |
| Gut movement and secretion | Decreased | Increased |
| Sphincters of gut and bladder | Contract | Relax |
| Urinary bladder wall | Relaxes (urine retained) | Contracts (urination) |
| Liver | Glycogen breakdown → blood glucose rises | Glycogen formation |
| Adrenal medulla | Releases adrenaline | — |
| Sweat glands | Sweating | — |

**Drug link:** atropine blocks parasympathetic (muscarinic) effects and dilates the pupil; salbutamol copies sympathetic action on bronchi; beta blockers reduce sympathetic action on the heart.

## Remember

- CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs.
- Dendrites → cell body → axon; myelin speeds conduction (saltatory).
- Cerebrum lobes: frontal (motor, Broca's speech), parietal (sensation), temporal (hearing), occipital (vision).
- Cerebellum = balance and coordination; damage → ataxia.
- Hypothalamus = temperature, hunger, thirst, ADH, controls pituitary and ANS.
- Medulla = cardiac, vasomotor, respiratory and reflex centres.
- Basal ganglia = smooth movement; dopamine loss → Parkinson's disease.
- Spinal cord ends at L1–L2; dorsal root sensory, ventral root motor; knee jerk is monosynaptic.
- Vagus (X) is the main parasympathetic nerve.
- Sympathetic = thoracolumbar, noradrenaline, fight or flight; parasympathetic = craniosacral, ACh, rest and digest.

# Unit 8: Sense organs

Syllabus chapter 12: anatomy and physiology of the eye, ear, skin, tongue and nose.

Sense organs contain **receptors** that change a stimulus (light, sound, touch, chemicals) into nerve impulses, which travel to the brain where the sensation is felt.

| Sense | Organ | Receptor type | Cranial nerve |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vision | Eye | Photoreceptors (rods, cones) | II (optic) |
| Hearing and balance | Ear | Mechanoreceptors (hair cells) | VIII (vestibulocochlear) |
| Touch, pain, temperature | Skin | Mechano-, thermo-, nociceptors | Spinal and trigeminal nerves |
| Taste (gustation) | Tongue | Chemoreceptors (taste buds) | VII, IX (X) |
| Smell (olfaction) | Nose | Chemoreceptors (olfactory cells) | I (olfactory) |

## 8.1 The eye

### Accessory structures

- **Eyebrows and eyelashes** – keep out sweat and dust.
- **Eyelids** – protect; blinking spreads tears.
- **Conjunctiva** – thin mucous membrane lining the lids and covering the white of the eye (inflammation = conjunctivitis).
- **Lacrimal apparatus** – lacrimal gland (upper outer part of the orbit) makes **tears**, which drain through the lacrimal canals and nasolacrimal duct into the nose. Tears moisten and clean the eye and contain **lysozyme** (antibacterial).
- **Six extrinsic eye muscles** – move the eyeball (supplied by cranial nerves III, IV, VI).

### Structure of the eyeball

```text
                     EYEBALL (horizontal section)

                        SCLERA (white, outer)
                ___________________________________
              /   choroid (vascular, dark)          \
             /    retina (inner, nerve layer)         \
   CORNEA   |                                           |
  (clear)   |   aqueous     LENS       VITREOUS         |
   _____    |   humour  ____/  \____   HUMOUR           |  FOVEA (in macula
  (     )   |  (ant.   |   (o)     |   (jelly)          |  = sharpest vision)
  (  pupil  |  chamber)|___ \__/ __|                    |  BLIND SPOT (optic disc)
  (_____)   |        IRIS   ciliary body +              |---- OPTIC NERVE --→ brain
             \               suspensory ligaments       /
              \_________________________________________/
```

The wall has **three layers (tunics):**

| Layer | Parts | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Outer fibrous** | **Sclera** (white, tough) behind; **cornea** (transparent, no blood vessels) in front | Protects and shapes the eye; cornea bends (refracts) light most |
| **Middle vascular (uvea)** | **Choroid** (blood vessels, dark pigment), **ciliary body** (ciliary muscle + processes), **iris** (coloured, with the pupil) | Nourishes; absorbs stray light; ciliary muscle changes lens shape; ciliary processes make aqueous humour; iris controls pupil size |
| **Inner nervous** | **Retina** – photoreceptors (rods and cones), bipolar cells, ganglion cells | Converts light into nerve impulses |

**Contents (refracting media):**

- **Aqueous humour** – watery fluid in front of the lens; made by the ciliary processes and drained through the **canal of Schlemm**; nourishes cornea and lens; maintains pressure (normal intraocular pressure about 10–21 mmHg). Poor drainage raises pressure → **glaucoma**.
- **Lens** – transparent, biconvex, elastic; held by suspensory ligaments; focuses light on the retina. Clouding = **cataract**.
- **Vitreous humour** – clear jelly behind the lens; keeps the eyeball's shape and holds the retina in place.

**Rods and cones**

| Rods | Cones |
| --- | --- |
| About 120 million; mostly at the periphery | About 6–7 million; most dense in the **fovea** |
| Work in **dim light** (night vision) | Work in **bright light** |
| Black-and-white vision | **Colour vision** (red, green, blue types) |
| Pigment **rhodopsin** (needs **vitamin A**) | Pigments iodopsins |

- **Macula lutea** with the **fovea centralis** – only cones; sharpest vision.
- **Optic disc (blind spot)** – where the optic nerve leaves; no rods or cones, so no image is seen there.

### Physiology of vision

1. Light passes through **cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina**.
2. The cornea and lens **refract** the light to form a real, **inverted**, smaller image on the retina.
3. Light breaks down rhodopsin in rods (and pigments in cones) → nerve impulses in the photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → **optic nerve**.
4. Optic nerves cross partly at the **optic chiasma** → optic tracts → thalamus → **visual cortex in the occipital lobe**, where the image is seen upright and in 3D.

- **Accommodation** – focusing on near objects: the ciliary muscle contracts, suspensory ligaments slacken, the lens becomes more convex; at the same time the pupil constricts and the eyes converge. For distant objects the ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens.
- **Pupillary light reflex** – bright light → pupil constricts (parasympathetic, circular muscle of iris); dim light → pupil dilates (sympathetic, radial muscle).
- **Night blindness** – vitamin A deficiency (less rhodopsin).

**Defects of vision**

| Defect | Problem | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Myopia** (short sight) | Eyeball too long; image forms in front of the retina; distant objects blurred | Concave lens |
| **Hypermetropia** (long sight) | Eyeball too short; image behind the retina; near objects blurred | Convex lens |
| **Presbyopia** | Lens loses elasticity with age; poor near vision | Convex (reading) lens |
| **Astigmatism** | Uneven curvature of cornea | Cylindrical lens |
| **Cataract** | Opaque lens | Surgery |
| **Glaucoma** | Raised pressure damages the optic nerve | Drops that lower pressure (e.g. timolol, pilocarpine) |

## 8.2 The ear

The ear has two jobs: **hearing** and **balance (equilibrium)**.

```text
                         EAR (section)

  OUTER EAR          |  MIDDLE EAR           |  INNER EAR
                     |  (air-filled)         |  (fluid-filled)
   pinna             |   malleus incus       |   semicircular canals (balance)
    ___              |      \    /  stapes   |       ( ) ( ) ( )
   (   \__ external  |     [M]--[I]--[S]-----|--oval window
   (    __ auditory  |                       |   vestibule (utricle, saccule)
   (___/   canal ===|| tympanic membrane     |   COCHLEA (snail-shaped,
           (wax)    ||                       |    organ of Corti = hearing)
                     |   Eustachian tube     |   round window
                     |   → to nasopharynx    |   → vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII)
```

### Parts of the ear

| Part | Structures | Functions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **External ear** | **Pinna (auricle)** of elastic cartilage; **external auditory canal** (about 2.5 cm) with ceruminous glands (wax) and hairs | Collects and directs sound waves; wax and hairs protect |
| **Middle ear** (tympanic cavity in the temporal bone) | **Tympanic membrane (eardrum)**; three **ossicles** – **malleus** (hammer), **incus** (anvil), **stapes** (stirrup – smallest bone of the body, fits the oval window); **Eustachian (auditory) tube** to the nasopharynx | Transmits and amplifies vibrations; Eustachian tube equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum |
| **Internal ear** (labyrinth) | Bony labyrinth filled with **perilymph** enclosing a membranous labyrinth filled with **endolymph**: **cochlea**, **vestibule** (utricle and saccule), **three semicircular canals** | Cochlea – hearing; vestibule and semicircular canals – balance |

**Cochlea:** spiral tube of about 2¾ turns with three channels (scala vestibuli, scala media, scala tympani). The **organ of Corti** on the basilar membrane carries **hair cells** – the receptors for hearing.

### Physiology of hearing

```text
 Sound waves → pinna → external canal → tympanic membrane vibrates
   → malleus → incus → stapes (amplify) → oval window
   → waves in perilymph and endolymph of the cochlea
   → basilar membrane vibrates → hair cells of organ of Corti bend
   → nerve impulses in cochlear nerve (VIII)
   → auditory cortex (temporal lobe) → sound is heard
   (round window bulges out to release the pressure)
```

- High-pitched sounds stimulate the base of the cochlea; low-pitched sounds the apex.
- Humans hear roughly 20–20,000 Hz.

### Physiology of balance

- **Utricle and saccule** (each with a **macula**: hair cells under a gel with tiny calcium carbonate crystals, **otoliths**) – sense **static equilibrium** (head position) and straight-line acceleration.
- **Semicircular canals** (three, at right angles to each other) – each has an **ampulla** with a **crista ampullaris**; endolymph movement bends the hair cells – sense **rotation of the head (dynamic equilibrium)**.
- Impulses go by the vestibular nerve to the brainstem and **cerebellum**, which adjust posture and eye movements.
- Disorders: motion sickness, vertigo, deafness (conductive or nerve), otitis media (middle-ear infection, common in children).

## 8.3 The skin

The skin (integument) is the **largest organ** of the body (about 1.5–2 m² area).

```text
                     SKIN (section)

    hair shaft   sweat pore
       |            |
  _____|____________|_______________  EPIDERMIS (stratified squamous
 |  stratum corneum (dead keratin)  |   keratinised; no blood vessels)
 |  ... granulosum, spinosum        |
 |  stratum basale (dividing cells, |
 |  MELANOCYTES)                    |
 |=====================================  dermal papillae
 |  DERMIS (connective tissue):         - blood vessels, nerves
 |   - sebaceous gland → into follicle  - Meissner's corpuscles (touch)
 |   - hair follicle + arrector pili    - free nerve endings (pain, temp)
 |   - sweat gland (coiled)             - Pacinian corpuscles (deep
 |_____________________________________   pressure, vibration)
 |  HYPODERMIS (subcutaneous fat)    |
```

**Layers**

1. **Epidermis** – outer stratified squamous keratinised epithelium; no blood vessels. Layers from deep to surface: stratum **basale** (germinativum – dividing cells and **melanocytes** making the pigment **melanin**), spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin of palms and soles only), **corneum** (dead flat cells full of **keratin**, constantly shed).
2. **Dermis** – dense connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibres, blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves, sensory receptors, hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands.
3. **Hypodermis (subcutaneous layer)** – fat and loose tissue (not strictly part of the skin) – insulation, energy store; site for subcutaneous injections.

**Appendages:** hair (keratin; arrector pili muscle causes "goose bumps"), nails, **sebaceous glands** (oily **sebum** – keeps hair and skin soft; blocked glands → acne), **sweat glands** – eccrine (all over, temperature control) and apocrine (armpit, groin; odour after bacterial action).

**Sensory receptors in the skin:** Meissner's corpuscles (light touch), Pacinian corpuscles (pressure, vibration), Merkel discs (touch), Ruffini endings (stretch), **free nerve endings** (pain and temperature).

**Functions of the skin**

1. **Protection** – barrier against microbes, chemicals, injury, water loss; melanin protects from UV rays.
2. **Temperature regulation** – sweating and changes in skin blood flow.
3. **Sensation** – touch, pressure, pain, heat and cold.
4. **Vitamin D synthesis** – sunlight (UV) converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin.
5. **Excretion** – small amounts of salts, urea in sweat.
6. **Absorption** – some fat-soluble substances and drugs (ointments, **transdermal patches** such as nitroglycerin, nicotine).
7. **Storage** – fat in the hypodermis.
8. Immunity – Langerhans cells in the epidermis.

## 8.4 The tongue (taste)

- Muscular organ in the floor of the mouth covered by mucous membrane with projections called **papillae**:
  - **Filiform** – most numerous, no taste buds (give a rough surface).
  - **Fungiform** – mushroom-shaped, on the tip and sides, some taste buds.
  - **Circumvallate (vallate)** – largest, 8–12 in a V-shaped row at the back, many taste buds.
  - **Foliate** – on the sides at the back.
- **Taste buds** contain **gustatory (taste) receptor cells** with taste hairs projecting through a taste pore, plus supporting cells.
- **Five basic tastes:** sweet, sour, salty, bitter, **umami** (savoury, e.g. glutamate). Each taste can be sensed over most of the tongue (the old "tongue map" is not accurate).
- **Physiology:** substances must **dissolve in saliva** → bind receptors → impulses through the **facial nerve (VII, front two-thirds)** and **glossopharyngeal nerve (IX, back third)** (and vagus from the throat) → medulla → thalamus → **gustatory cortex**.
- **Functions of the tongue:** taste, chewing and mixing food with saliva, swallowing, speech, cleaning the teeth.
- Much of "flavour" comes from smell; a blocked nose dulls taste.

## 8.5 The nose (smell)

- The **olfactory epithelium** lies in the roof of the nasal cavity (a small area of a few cm²). It contains **olfactory receptor cells** (bipolar neurons with cilia in the mucus), supporting cells and basal (stem) cells. Olfactory receptor cells are one of the few neurons that are replaced throughout life.
- **Physiology:** odour molecules **dissolve in nasal mucus** → bind receptors on the olfactory hairs → impulses travel through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the **olfactory nerve (I)** → **olfactory bulb** → olfactory tract → **olfactory cortex in the temporal lobe** and limbic system (so smell is linked to memory and emotion). Smell does not pass through the thalamus first.
- Receptors **adapt quickly** – a constant smell soon stops being noticed.
- **Other functions of the nose:** passage of air, filtering, warming and moistening air, voice resonance.
- Loss of smell = **anosmia** (colds, head injury, some viral infections).

## Remember

- Eye wall: fibrous (sclera, cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), nervous (retina).
- Rods = dim light (rhodopsin, vitamin A); cones = colour, concentrated in the fovea; optic disc = blind spot.
- Accommodation for near vision: ciliary muscle contracts, lens bulges.
- Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens; glaucoma = raised eye pressure; cataract = opaque lens.
- Ear: outer (pinna, canal), middle (eardrum, malleus–incus–stapes, Eustachian tube), inner (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals).
- Organ of Corti = hearing; semicircular canals = rotation; utricle and saccule = head position.
- Skin = largest organ; epidermis (melanin, keratin), dermis (glands, receptors); makes vitamin D.
- Taste buds: VII (front two-thirds), IX (back third); five tastes including umami.
- Smell: olfactory nerve (I) through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.

# Unit 9: Urinary system

Syllabus chapter 13: anatomy and physiology of the urinary system; physiology of urine formation; renin–angiotensin system; clearance tests and micturition.

The urinary system removes wastes from the blood and keeps the volume, composition and pH of body fluids constant.

**Organs:** two **kidneys** (make urine), two **ureters** (carry urine), one **urinary bladder** (stores urine), one **urethra** (passes urine out).

## 9.1 Kidneys – gross anatomy

- Bean-shaped, reddish-brown organs, each about 11 cm long, 6 cm wide, 3 cm thick and about 150 g.
- Lie on the posterior abdominal wall **behind the peritoneum (retroperitoneal)**, one on each side of the vertebral column, from about T12 to L3. The **right kidney is slightly lower** because the liver lies above it.
- The **adrenal gland** sits on top of each kidney.
- The medial concave border has the **hilum**, where the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave.
- Coverings: fibrous **renal capsule**, a layer of fat, and renal fascia.

```text
                 KIDNEY (longitudinal section)

            ___________________________
           /  capsule                   \
          /  CORTEX (outer, granular)    \
         |   ___     ___     ___          |
         |  /   \   /   \   /   \  <- renal pyramids (MEDULLA)
         | | ||| | | ||| | | ||| |        |   striped, apex = papilla
         |  \_v_/   \_v_/   \_v_/         |
         |    \ minor calyx /     renal   |
         |     \___________/      columns |
         |       MAJOR CALYX              |
          \        \ RENAL PELVIS ========= HILUM
           \        \________ ureter ↓    | renal artery in,
            \___________________________/   renal vein out
```

**Internal parts**

1. **Cortex** – outer granular layer; contains glomeruli and convoluted tubules.
2. **Medulla** – inner part made of 8–18 cone-shaped **renal pyramids** (striped because of loops of Henle and collecting ducts); their tips (**papillae**) open into the calyces. **Renal columns** are cortex extending between pyramids.
3. **Minor calyces → major calyces → renal pelvis → ureter.**

**Blood supply:** the kidneys receive about **1.2 litres of blood per minute (about 20–25 % of cardiac output)**.
Renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular arteries → **afferent arteriole** → **glomerulus** → **efferent arteriole** → **peritubular capillaries** (and vasa recta around loops of Henle) → veins → renal vein.

## 9.2 Nephron – the functional unit

Each kidney has about **1 million nephrons**.

```text
                 NEPHRON (draw and label – 10 marks)

    afferent arteriole →  ___
    efferent arteriole ← (GLOMERULUS)  ← tuft of capillaries
                         \  BOWMAN'S /    } RENAL CORPUSCLE
                          \_CAPSULE_/     } (in cortex)
                               |
                  PROXIMAL CONVOLUTED TUBULE (PCT)   ~~~~ (cortex)
                               |
                 DESCENDING LIMB  |        ^  ASCENDING LIMB
                    of loop       |        |  (thick part pumps
                                  |        |   Na+, Cl− out)
                                  \___U___/  LOOP OF HENLE (medulla)
                                           |
                  DISTAL CONVOLUTED TUBULE (DCT) ~~~~ (cortex)
                     (macula densa next to afferent arteriole =
                      juxtaglomerular apparatus)
                                           |
                                  COLLECTING DUCT → papilla → calyx
                                  (several nephrons share one)
```

| Part | Structure | Main job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Glomerulus** | Tuft of capillaries between afferent (wider) and efferent (narrower) arterioles | Filtration |
| **Bowman's capsule** | Double-walled cup; inner layer of **podocytes** | Collects filtrate |
| **Proximal convoluted tubule** | Cuboidal cells with brush border (microvilli), many mitochondria | Reabsorbs most water and solutes |
| **Loop of Henle** | Descending (permeable to water) and ascending (permeable to salts, not water) limbs | Concentration of urine (counter-current) |
| **Distal convoluted tubule** | Shorter, fewer microvilli | Fine adjustment under hormones (aldosterone); K+ and H+ secretion |
| **Collecting duct** | Receives several DCTs | Water reabsorption under **ADH** |

- **Cortical nephrons** (about 85 %) have short loops; **juxtamedullary nephrons** have long loops reaching deep into the medulla and help make concentrated urine.
- **Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA):** **juxtaglomerular cells** (modified smooth muscle in the wall of the afferent arteriole; secrete **renin**) + **macula densa** (special DCT cells that sense Na+/Cl−). Controls GFR and BP.

## 9.3 Physiology of urine formation

Urine is formed in three steps:

```text
  BLOOD in glomerulus
        ↓ 1. GLOMERULAR FILTRATION (glomerulus → Bowman's capsule)
  FILTRATE (~180 L/day)
        ↓ 2. TUBULAR REABSORPTION (tubule → blood): ~99 % returned
        ↓ 3. TUBULAR SECRETION (blood → tubule): H+, K+, drugs added
  URINE (~1–1.5 L/day)
```

### Step 1: Glomerular filtration

- Blood plasma is filtered through the **filtration membrane** (capillary endothelium with pores + basement membrane + filtration slits between podocytes).
- **Filtered:** water, glucose, amino acids, salts, urea, creatinine, uric acid, small drugs.
- **Not filtered:** blood cells and plasma proteins (too large). So the filtrate is plasma without proteins.
- **Driving force – net filtration pressure (approximate values):**

| Pressure | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure | About 55 mmHg | Pushes fluid out (favours filtration) |
| Plasma colloid osmotic pressure | About 30 mmHg | Pulls fluid back (opposes) |
| Capsular hydrostatic pressure | About 15 mmHg | Opposes |
| **Net filtration pressure** | 55 − (30 + 15) ≈ **10 mmHg** | — |

- Glomerular pressure is high because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent.
- **Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** ≈ **125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day** in a healthy adult.
- GFR falls if BP falls very low (shock) or in kidney disease; it is kept fairly steady over a wide BP range by **autoregulation**.

### Step 2: Tubular reabsorption

About 99 % of the filtrate goes back into the blood (peritubular capillaries).

| Site | What is reabsorbed |
| --- | --- |
| **PCT** (most, about 65 % of filtrate) | All **glucose** and **amino acids** (active), most Na+ (active), Cl−, K+, HCO3−, water (osmosis), some urea |
| **Descending limb of loop** | Water |
| **Ascending limb** | Na+, Cl−, K+ (not water) → makes the medulla salty (hypertonic) |
| **DCT** | Na+ (under **aldosterone**, exchanged for K+), Ca2+ (under parathormone), water |
| **Collecting duct** | Water (under **ADH**), urea (inner medulla) |

- **Renal threshold for glucose** ≈ 180 mg/dL: above this blood level, carriers are saturated and glucose appears in urine (**glycosuria**, as in diabetes mellitus).
- **ADH** makes collecting ducts permeable to water → small volume of concentrated urine. No ADH → large volume of dilute urine (**diabetes insipidus**).

### Step 3: Tubular secretion

Substances are moved from the peritubular blood into the tubule: **H+** and **NH4+** (keeps blood pH normal), **K+** (DCT, under aldosterone), creatinine, and many **drugs** (penicillin, para-aminohippuric acid). This removes substances quickly and helps acid–base balance.

### Normal urine

| Property | Normal |
| --- | --- |
| Volume | About 1–1.5 L/day (varies with intake) |
| Colour | Pale yellow (urochrome) |
| pH | About 6 (range about 4.5–8) |
| Specific gravity | About 1.010–1.025 |
| Contents | About 95 % water; urea (main solid), creatinine, uric acid, Na+, K+, Cl−, phosphates |
| Abnormal | Glucose, proteins (albumin), blood, ketones, bile pigments, pus cells |

**Functions of the kidney (summary):** excretion of wastes (urea, creatinine, uric acid, drugs); water and electrolyte balance; acid–base balance; BP control (renin); RBC production (**erythropoietin**); activation of **vitamin D** (calcitriol); gluconeogenesis in starvation.

## 9.4 Renin–angiotensin system (RAAS)

```text
  BP ↓ / blood volume ↓ / Na+ ↓ at macula densa / sympathetic stimulation
        ↓
  JG cells of the kidney release RENIN (enzyme)
        ↓
  ANGIOTENSINOGEN (plasma protein from the liver)
        ↓  renin
  ANGIOTENSIN I (inactive)
        ↓  ANGIOTENSIN-CONVERTING ENZYME (ACE) – mainly in the lungs
  ANGIOTENSIN II (active)
        ↓
   ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
   Strong         Adrenal cortex →        Thirst ↑ and           Posterior pituitary
   VASOCONSTRICTION  ALDOSTERONE →        drinking               → ADH → water
   (resistance ↑)    Na+ and water                                retention
                     retained, K+ lost
   └──────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
        ↓
  Blood volume and BP RISE → renin release falls (negative feedback)
```

**Importance:** maintains BP, blood volume and Na+ balance. Over-activity causes **hypertension**. Drugs: **ACE inhibitors** (enalapril, ramipril), **angiotensin receptor blockers** (losartan), aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone).

## 9.5 Clearance tests

**Renal clearance** of a substance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of that substance by the kidneys per minute.

**Formula:** C = (U × V) ÷ P

- C = clearance (mL/min)
- U = concentration of the substance in urine (mg/mL)
- V = urine flow rate (mL/min)
- P = concentration in plasma (mg/mL)

**Worked example:** creatinine in urine 1.2 mg/mL, urine flow 1.0 mL/min, plasma creatinine 0.01 mg/mL → C = (1.2 × 1.0) ÷ 0.01 = **120 mL/min** (normal).

| Test | What it measures | Approximate normal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inulin clearance** | Exact GFR (inulin is filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted) | About 125 mL/min |
| **Creatinine clearance** | Practical estimate of GFR (endogenous, no injection needed) | About 110–125 mL/min |
| **Urea clearance** | Kidney function (urea partly reabsorbed, so value is lower than GFR) | About 70 mL/min |
| **PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) clearance** | Effective renal plasma flow (filtered and secreted almost completely) | About 600–650 mL/min |

**Uses:** assess kidney function, detect early kidney disease, and **adjust drug doses** in renal impairment (important for pharmacists – e.g. aminoglycosides, digoxin). Blood urea and serum creatinine are simple blood tests that also rise in kidney failure.

## 9.6 Ureters, urinary bladder and urethra

- **Ureters:** two muscular tubes about 25–30 cm long from the renal pelvis to the bladder; urine moves by **peristalsis**; they enter the bladder obliquely, which prevents back-flow.
- **Urinary bladder:** hollow muscular bag in the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis. Wall of smooth **detrusor muscle**; lining of **transitional epithelium** (stretches); the **trigone** is the smooth triangular area between the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening. Normally holds about 400–600 mL comfortably.
- **Urethra:** carries urine out. **Female** – about 4 cm (short, so urinary infections are more common in women). **Male** – about 18–20 cm, also carries semen; passes through the prostate and penis.
- **Sphincters:** **internal urethral sphincter** (smooth muscle, involuntary) and **external urethral sphincter** (skeletal muscle, voluntary, supplied by the pudendal nerve).

## 9.7 Micturition

**Micturition** (urination) is the emptying of the urinary bladder. It is a **spinal reflex** controlled by higher brain centres.

```text
  Bladder fills → stretch receptors in the wall (urge felt at about
  200–400 mL)
        ↓  sensory impulses (pelvic nerves)
  Micturition centre in the SACRAL spinal cord (S2–S4)
        ↓  parasympathetic (pelvic) nerves
  DETRUSOR CONTRACTS + internal sphincter relaxes
        ↓
  Impulses also reach the brain (pons, cortex) → person decides:
   - convenient → external sphincter relaxed voluntarily → URINE PASSED
   - not convenient → external sphincter kept closed, reflex inhibited
```

- **Sympathetic** nerves relax the detrusor and close the internal sphincter (help storage).
- **Infants** have no voluntary control until the nerve pathways mature (about 2–3 years).
- **Disorders:** **incontinence** (loss of control – old age, spinal injury), **retention** (cannot empty – enlarged prostate, after surgery), cystitis, kidney stones (renal calculi).

**Common kidney disorders:** renal failure (acute, chronic – needs dialysis), glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome (heavy protein loss), urinary tract infection.

## Remember

- Kidneys are retroperitoneal, T12–L3; right kidney lower; adrenal on top.
- Nephron = renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) + PCT + loop of Henle + DCT → collecting duct; about 1 million per kidney.
- Urine formation: filtration → reabsorption → secretion.
- GFR ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day; urine ≈ 1.5 L/day; net filtration pressure ≈ 10 mmHg.
- PCT reabsorbs all glucose and amino acids; renal threshold for glucose ≈ 180 mg/dL.
- ADH → water reabsorption in collecting duct; aldosterone → Na+ in, K+ out in DCT.
- RAAS: renin → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone.
- Clearance C = UV/P; inulin = GFR; PAH = renal plasma flow.
- Micturition reflex centre S2–S4; parasympathetic contracts the detrusor; external sphincter voluntary.

# Unit 10: Endocrine system

Syllabus chapter 14: hormones and their functions – pituitary gland, adrenal gland, thyroid and parathyroid glands, pancreas and gonads.

## 10.1 Introduction

- **Endocrine glands** are **ductless** glands that release chemical messengers called **hormones** directly into the blood, which carries them to **target cells** with matching **receptors**.
- Exocrine glands, by contrast, pour secretions through ducts (salivary, sweat glands). The **pancreas** and **gonads** are both endocrine and exocrine (**mixed glands**).
- The endocrine system works **slowly but its effects last longer** than nervous control; together they keep homeostasis. The **hypothalamus** links the two systems.

**Chemical types of hormones**

| Type | Examples | How they act |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amino acid derivatives (amines) | Adrenaline, noradrenaline, thyroxine (T3, T4) | Catecholamines act on membrane receptors; thyroid hormones enter the cell |
| Peptides and proteins | Insulin, glucagon, GH, ADH, oxytocin, PTH, TSH | Bind membrane receptors → second messenger (e.g. cyclic AMP) inside the cell |
| Steroids (from cholesterol) | Cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone | Lipid-soluble; enter the cell, bind receptors in cytoplasm or nucleus → change gene expression |

**Control of secretion:** mostly **negative feedback** (e.g. high thyroxine suppresses TSH), plus nervous control (adrenal medulla) and blood levels of substances (glucose → insulin; Ca2+ → PTH).

```text
     Main endocrine glands (front view)

          hypothalamus
          PITUITARY  (base of brain)
          pineal gland
          THYROID + 4 PARATHYROIDS (neck)
          thymus (chest)
          ADRENALS (on top of kidneys)
          PANCREAS – islets (behind stomach)
          OVARIES (female pelvis) / TESTES (scrotum)
```

## 10.2 Pituitary gland (hypophysis)

- Pea-sized gland (about 0.5 g) in the **sella turcica** of the sphenoid bone, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk (**infundibulum**).
- Called the "**master gland**" because it controls several other glands – but it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus.
- Two lobes:

**Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)** – glandular; controlled by **releasing and inhibiting hormones** from the hypothalamus carried in the **hypophyseal portal veins**.

| Hormone | Target | Main actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Growth hormone (GH, somatotropin)** | Most tissues, bone, muscle, liver | Growth of bones and muscles (through IGF-1 from the liver); protein synthesis; raises blood glucose; fat breakdown |
| **Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** | Thyroid | Release of T3 and T4; growth of thyroid |
| **Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)** | Adrenal cortex | Release of cortisol (glucocorticoids) |
| **Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)** | Ovary / testis | Female: growth of ovarian follicles, oestrogen secretion. Male: spermatogenesis |
| **Luteinising hormone (LH)** (ICSH in males) | Ovary / testis | Female: **ovulation**, forms corpus luteum (progesterone). Male: testosterone from Leydig cells |
| **Prolactin** | Breast | Milk production after childbirth |
| (Melanocyte-stimulating hormone) | Skin | Pigmentation |

**Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)** – nervous tissue; **stores and releases** two hormones **made in the hypothalamus**:

| Hormone | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| **Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** | Water reabsorption in kidney collecting ducts → less, concentrated urine; vasoconstriction in large doses |
| **Oxytocin** | Contraction of the uterus during labour (positive feedback); milk ejection ("let-down") during suckling |

**Disorders**

- **GH excess:** in children – **gigantism**; in adults – **acromegaly** (enlarged hands, feet, jaw).
- **GH deficiency in children:** **pituitary dwarfism** (short but well-proportioned, normal intelligence).
- **ADH deficiency:** **diabetes insipidus** – large volumes of dilute urine, thirst.

## 10.3 Thyroid gland

- Butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck, below the larynx: two **lobes** joined by an **isthmus** in front of the trachea; about 20–30 g.
- Made of many spherical **follicles** lined by cuboidal cells and filled with **colloid** (thyroglobulin – stored hormone). **Parafollicular (C) cells** lie between follicles.

**Hormones**

| Hormone | From | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Thyroxine (T4)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)** – contain **iodine**; T3 is more active | Follicular cells | Raise the **basal metabolic rate (BMR)**, O2 use and heat production; needed for normal **growth and brain development** in children; increase heart rate; help carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism |
| **Calcitonin** | Parafollicular (C) cells | **Lowers blood calcium** by reducing bone resorption (opposes PTH) |

- **Iodine** from food (iodised salt) is essential to make T3 and T4.
- **Control:** hypothalamus (TRH) → anterior pituitary (TSH) → thyroid (T3, T4); high T3/T4 inhibit TRH and TSH (negative feedback).

**Disorders**

| Condition | Features |
| --- | --- |
| **Hypothyroidism – cretinism** (in infants/children) | Stunted growth, mental retardation, coarse features, protruding tongue |
| **Hypothyroidism – myxoedema** (adults) | Low BMR, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, puffy face, sluggishness |
| **Hyperthyroidism – Graves' disease** | High BMR, weight loss, heat intolerance, nervousness, fast heart rate, **exophthalmos** (bulging eyes) |
| **Simple (endemic) goitre** | Enlarged thyroid from **iodine deficiency** (common in hilly areas – prevented by iodised salt) |

## 10.4 Parathyroid glands

- **Four** small glands (two pairs) on the **back of the thyroid** lobes.
- Secrete **parathormone (PTH)** – the main hormone that **raises blood calcium**.

**Actions of PTH**

1. **Bone:** stimulates osteoclasts → calcium and phosphate released from bone.
2. **Kidney:** increases calcium reabsorption, increases phosphate excretion; activates **vitamin D** (calcitriol).
3. **Intestine:** (through calcitriol) increases calcium absorption.

Normal blood calcium is about 9–11 mg/dL. Low Ca2+ stimulates PTH; high Ca2+ stimulates calcitonin.

**Disorders:** **hypoparathyroidism** (e.g. accidental removal in thyroid surgery) → low calcium → **tetany** (muscle spasms, tingling, carpopedal spasm). **Hyperparathyroidism** → high calcium, weak bones (decalcification), kidney stones.

## 10.5 Adrenal (suprarenal) glands

- Two triangular glands, one **on top of each kidney**.
- Each has an outer **cortex** (about 80 %, from mesoderm, makes steroids) and an inner **medulla** (from nervous tissue, part of the sympathetic system).

```text
     ADRENAL GLAND (section)

   capsule
   ┌─────────────────────────────┐
   │ Zona glomerulosa → MINERALOCORTICOIDS (aldosterone)     "Salt"
   │ Zona fasciculata → GLUCOCORTICOIDS (cortisol)           "Sugar"
   │ Zona reticularis → SEX HORMONES (androgens)             "Sex"
   │   ┌───────────────────┐
   │   │ MEDULLA → adrenaline (≈80 %), noradrenaline          │
   │   └───────────────────┘
   └─────────────────────────────┘
   Memory: "Salt, Sugar, Sex – the deeper you go, the sweeter it gets"
```

**Adrenal cortex hormones**

| Group | Main hormone | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mineralocorticoids** | **Aldosterone** | Na+ and water reabsorption and K+ excretion in the DCT and collecting duct → raises blood volume and BP. Controlled mainly by the **renin–angiotensin system** and blood K+ |
| **Glucocorticoids** | **Cortisol (hydrocortisone)** | Raises blood glucose (gluconeogenesis); protein breakdown; fat redistribution; **anti-inflammatory** and **immunosuppressive**; helps the body resist **stress**. Controlled by ACTH (with a morning peak) |
| **Sex hormones** | Androgens (small amounts) | Pubic and axillary hair; sex drive in females |

**Adrenal medulla hormones – adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine)**

- Released in response to sympathetic stimulation during stress, fear, exercise – the "**fight or flight**" response.
- Actions: increase heart rate and force, raise BP, dilate bronchi, raise blood glucose (glycogen breakdown), dilate pupils, divert blood to muscles, reduce gut activity.

**Disorders**

| Disorder | Cause | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Addison's disease** | Low cortisol and aldosterone (cortex destroyed) | Weakness, weight loss, low BP, low blood sugar, **bronze pigmentation** of skin |
| **Cushing's syndrome** | Excess cortisol (tumour or long-term steroid drugs) | **Moon face**, buffalo hump, central obesity, purple stretch marks, high BP, high blood sugar, weak bones |
| **Conn's syndrome** (primary aldosteronism) | Excess aldosterone | High BP, low K+ |
| **Phaeochromocytoma** | Tumour of adrenal medulla | Episodes of very high BP, palpitations, sweating |

## 10.6 Pancreas (endocrine part)

- The **islets of Langerhans** – about a million small clusters of cells scattered among the exocrine acini (about 1–2 % of the pancreas).

| Cell | Proportion (approx.) | Hormone | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Alpha (α)** | 20 % | **Glucagon** | **Raises blood glucose**: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver |
| **Beta (β)** | 70 % | **Insulin** | **Lowers blood glucose**: helps glucose enter muscle and fat cells; glycogen formation in liver and muscle; fat and protein synthesis; stops gluconeogenesis |
| **Delta (δ)** | 5–10 % | **Somatostatin** | Inhibits insulin and glucagon release; slows digestion |
| PP (F) cells | Small | Pancreatic polypeptide | Regulates pancreatic secretion |

```text
   Blood glucose control (negative feedback)

  After a meal: glucose ↑ → β-cells → INSULIN → cells take up glucose,
                liver stores glycogen → glucose falls to normal
  Fasting:      glucose ↓ → α-cells → GLUCAGON → liver breaks glycogen,
                makes new glucose → glucose rises to normal

  Normal fasting blood glucose ≈ 70–100 mg/dL
```

**Diabetes mellitus** – high blood glucose from lack of insulin or poor response to it.

- **Type 1** – autoimmune destruction of β-cells; usually children and young adults; needs insulin injections.
- **Type 2** – insulin resistance (most common, adults, linked to obesity); treated with diet, exercise, oral drugs (metformin), sometimes insulin.
- **Features:** the "3 Ps" – **polyuria** (much urine), **polydipsia** (thirst), **polyphagia** (hunger); glycosuria; weight loss; ketoacidosis in severe type 1; long-term damage to eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels.
- **Hypoglycaemia** (too low glucose, e.g. insulin overdose) – sweating, tremor, confusion, coma.

## 10.7 Gonads

### Testes (male)

- **Leydig (interstitial) cells** between the seminiferous tubules secrete **testosterone** (under LH/ICSH).
- **Actions of testosterone:** development of male sex organs; **male secondary sexual characteristics** at puberty (beard, deep voice, muscle growth, body hair); spermatogenesis (with FSH); sex drive; protein building (anabolic).
- **Sertoli cells** secrete **inhibin** (inhibits FSH) and support sperm formation.

### Ovaries (female)

- **Oestrogens** (mainly oestradiol) from developing **follicles**: development of female sex organs and **female secondary sexual characteristics** (breast development, broad pelvis, fat distribution); growth of the uterine lining (proliferative phase); regulation of the menstrual cycle.
- **Progesterone** from the **corpus luteum** (and the placenta in pregnancy): prepares and maintains the uterine lining for implantation (secretory phase); maintains pregnancy; prepares breasts for milk; raises body temperature slightly after ovulation.
- **Relaxin** (pregnancy) – relaxes pelvic ligaments; **inhibin** – inhibits FSH.

**Control:** hypothalamus (GnRH) → anterior pituitary (FSH, LH) → gonads (sex hormones) → feedback to hypothalamus and pituitary. (Details of the cycle are in Unit 11.)

**Other endocrine tissues (for MCQs):** pineal gland (**melatonin** – sleep–wake rhythm), thymus (**thymosin** – T-cell maturation), kidney (erythropoietin, renin), heart (ANP), stomach and duodenum (gastrin, secretin, CCK), placenta (hCG).

## Remember

- Endocrine glands are ductless; hormones travel in blood to target cells.
- Anterior pituitary: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin. Posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin (made in the hypothalamus).
- GH excess: gigantism (child), acromegaly (adult); ADH lack: diabetes insipidus.
- Thyroid: T3, T4 (need iodine; raise BMR) and calcitonin (lowers Ca2+). Cretinism, myxoedema, Graves' disease, goitre.
- Parathyroids: PTH raises blood Ca2+; deficiency → tetany.
- Adrenal cortex: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens); medulla: adrenaline.
- Addison's = deficiency (bronze skin); Cushing's = cortisol excess (moon face).
- Islets: α → glucagon (raises glucose), β → insulin (lowers glucose), δ → somatostatin.
- Testes → testosterone (Leydig cells); ovaries → oestrogen (follicles), progesterone (corpus luteum).

# Unit 11: Reproductive system

Syllabus chapter 15: anatomy of the male and female reproductive systems; physiology of menstruation; spermatogenesis and oogenesis; pregnancy and parturition.

The reproductive system produces **gametes** (sperm and ova), **sex hormones**, and – in the female – supports the growing baby. The primary sex organs (**gonads**) are the testes and ovaries.

## 11.1 Male reproductive system

```text
            MALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM (side view, simplified)

                     urinary bladder
                          |  ____ seminal vesicle (behind bladder)
                 ureter→  | /
                          |/   ejaculatory duct
         vas deferens →  PROSTATE (around urethra)
         (from testis,       |  bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland
          over bladder)      |
                         URETHRA → through PENIS → external opening
                             |
         EPIDIDYMIS  ←  TESTIS (in SCROTUM)
         (coiled tube on      seminiferous tubules → sperm
          back of testis)     Leydig cells → testosterone
```

| Organ | Structure | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Scrotum** | Pouch of skin and muscle outside the body | Holds the testes about 2–3 °C below body temperature, which is needed for sperm production |
| **Testes** (2) | Oval glands about 4–5 cm long; each divided into lobules containing coiled **seminiferous tubules** (with **Sertoli cells**); **Leydig (interstitial) cells** between tubules | Produce **sperm** (spermatogenesis) and **testosterone** |
| **Epididymis** | Highly coiled tube (about 6 m long) on the back of each testis | Stores sperm while they **mature** and gain the ability to swim |
| **Vas deferens (ductus deferens)** | Muscular tube about 45 cm long, in the spermatic cord, through the inguinal canal | Carries sperm to the ejaculatory duct (cut in **vasectomy**) |
| **Seminal vesicles** (2) | Glands behind the bladder | Make about 60 % of semen: alkaline fluid with **fructose** (energy for sperm) and prostaglandins |
| **Ejaculatory ducts** | Formed by vas deferens + seminal vesicle duct | Pass through the prostate into the urethra |
| **Prostate gland** | Walnut-sized gland below the bladder, around the urethra | Milky, slightly acidic fluid (about 25–30 % of semen) with citric acid and enzymes; enlarges in old age (BPH → difficult urination) |
| **Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands** | Two pea-sized glands below the prostate | Mucus that lubricates and neutralises the urethra before ejaculation |
| **Urethra** | About 18–20 cm | Common passage for urine and semen |
| **Penis** | Root, shaft, glans; erectile tissue (corpora cavernosa, corpus spongiosum) | Copulatory organ; erection by filling with blood (parasympathetic) |

**Semen:** sperm + secretions of seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands. Volume about 2–5 mL per ejaculation; slightly alkaline.

**Structure of a sperm (spermatozoon):**

```text
   HEAD [acrosome cap + nucleus (23 chromosomes)] — NECK —
   MIDDLE PIECE (mitochondria → energy) ———— TAIL (flagellum → swimming)
```

The **acrosome** holds enzymes that help the sperm pass through the layers around the ovum.

## 11.2 Spermatogenesis

**Spermatogenesis** is the formation of sperm in the **seminiferous tubules**, from puberty onwards throughout life. It takes about 64–74 days.

```text
  Spermatogonium (2n = 46)  ← stem cells near the basement membrane;
        |   divide by MITOSIS (multiplication phase)
        ↓   growth
  Primary spermatocyte (2n = 46)
        |   MEIOSIS I
        ↓
  2 Secondary spermatocytes (n = 23)
        |   MEIOSIS II
        ↓
  4 Spermatids (n = 23)
        |   SPERMIOGENESIS (change in shape: acrosome, tail form;
        ↓   cytoplasm lost) – nourished by Sertoli cells
  4 Spermatozoa (n = 23) → released into the lumen → epididymis
```

- One primary spermatocyte gives **four** functional sperm.
- **Control:** FSH (with testosterone) stimulates spermatogenesis through Sertoli cells; LH stimulates testosterone from Leydig cells; inhibin from Sertoli cells feeds back to lower FSH.
- Sperm carry either an **X or a Y** chromosome, so the sperm decides the sex of the baby.

## 11.3 Female reproductive system

```text
           FEMALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM (front view)

     fimbriae    UTERINE (FALLOPIAN) TUBE          UTERINE TUBE
      \\\  ______________________   ____________________  ///
   OVARY (o)              \           /             (o) OVARY
     (ovarian ligament)    \ FUNDUS  /
                          |  BODY of   |  wall: perimetrium,
                          |  UTERUS    |  MYOMETRIUM (muscle),
                          |  (cavity)  |  ENDOMETRIUM (lining – shed
                           \          /   in menstruation)
                             \ CERVIX /
                              |      |
                              |VAGINA|
                              |______|
                           external genitalia (vulva)
```

| Organ | Structure | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ovaries** (2) | Almond-shaped, about 3 cm, in the pelvis on each side of the uterus; cortex with **ovarian follicles** at different stages | Produce **ova** (oogenesis) and the hormones **oestrogen** and **progesterone** |
| **Uterine (fallopian) tubes** (2) | About 10 cm long; parts: infundibulum with finger-like **fimbriae**, ampulla, isthmus; ciliated lining | Catch the ovum at ovulation; **fertilisation usually takes place in the ampulla**; cilia and peristalsis move the embryo to the uterus |
| **Uterus** | Hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ (about 7.5 cm long) between bladder and rectum; parts: fundus, body, cervix. Wall: **perimetrium** (outer), **myometrium** (thick smooth muscle), **endometrium** (inner lining) | Receives and nourishes the embryo (implantation); forms the maternal part of the placenta; contracts in labour; endometrium is shed in menstruation |
| **Cervix** | Narrow lower part of the uterus opening into the vagina | Mucus plug; dilates in labour |
| **Vagina** | Muscular tube about 8–10 cm; acidic secretions protect against infection | Receives the penis; birth canal; outlet for menstrual flow |
| **External genitalia (vulva)** | Mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris, vestibule | Protection; sexual sensation |
| **Mammary glands** (accessory) | Lobes of glandular tissue with ducts opening at the nipple | Milk production (prolactin) and ejection (oxytocin) |

## 11.4 Oogenesis

**Oogenesis** is the formation of ova in the ovaries.

```text
  BEFORE BIRTH (fetal ovary):
  Oogonia (2n) → mitosis → PRIMARY OOCYTES (2n) start meiosis I and
  STOP at prophase I; each in a primordial follicle. (About 1–2 million
  at birth; about 4 lakh by puberty – no new ones are made.)

  FROM PUBERTY, EACH MONTH (under FSH):
  Primary oocyte completes MEIOSIS I →
     SECONDARY OOCYTE (n) + FIRST POLAR BODY (small, degenerates)
        |
     OVULATION (secondary oocyte released, arrested at metaphase II)
        |
     Only IF a sperm enters (fertilisation): MEIOSIS II completes →
     OVUM (n) + SECOND POLAR BODY
```

- One primary oocyte gives **only one** functional ovum (plus polar bodies), unlike four sperm from one spermatocyte. The unequal division gives the ovum most of the cytoplasm (food for the early embryo).
- About 400–500 ova are released during a woman's reproductive life; the rest of the follicles degenerate (atresia).
- Oogenesis stops at **menopause** (about 45–50 years).
- Every ovum carries an **X** chromosome.

**Follicle development:** primordial → primary → secondary → mature **Graafian follicle** (fluid-filled antrum) → ruptures at ovulation → the remaining follicle becomes the **corpus luteum** (yellow body, secretes progesterone and oestrogen) → if no pregnancy, it degenerates into the **corpus albicans** (white scar).

## 11.5 Physiology of menstruation (menstrual cycle)

The **menstrual cycle** is the regular monthly series of changes in the ovary and uterus that prepares for pregnancy. Average length **28 days** (range about 21–35). It starts at puberty (**menarche**, about 11–14 years) and stops at **menopause**.

| Phase (28-day cycle) | Days | Ovary | Uterus (endometrium) | Hormones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Menstrual phase** | 1–5 | New follicles begin to grow | Functional layer of endometrium breaks down and is shed with blood (about 50–80 mL) | Oestrogen and progesterone low (corpus luteum has died) |
| **Proliferative (follicular) phase** | 6–13 | Follicles grow; one becomes the mature **Graafian follicle** | Endometrium **repairs and thickens**; glands and blood vessels grow | **FSH** ↑ → follicle makes **oestrogen** ↑ |
| **Ovulation** | About day 14 | Graafian follicle ruptures and releases the secondary oocyte | — | **LH surge** (triggered by high oestrogen – positive feedback) |
| **Secretory (luteal) phase** | 15–28 | **Corpus luteum** forms | Endometrium becomes thick, soft, rich in glands and blood vessels, ready for implantation | **Progesterone** ↑ (and oestrogen) from corpus luteum; FSH and LH suppressed |

```text
   HORMONE LEVELS DURING THE CYCLE (sketch)

  LH          .                   (sharp peak just before day 14)
             / \
  FSH  __.--'   '--.______________
  Oestrogen    /\ (peak before ovulation)   /‾‾\ (smaller rise)
  ____________/  \_________________________/    \____
  Progesterone                     ______
  ________________________________/      \___________
  Days: 1    5          14                 21         28
        |menses|proliferative|  ovulation |  secretory  |
```

- **If no fertilisation:** the corpus luteum degenerates after about 10–12 days → progesterone and oestrogen fall → the endometrium loses its support → **menstruation** begins; FSH rises again and a new cycle starts.
- **If fertilisation occurs:** the embryo makes **hCG** (human chorionic gonadotropin), which keeps the corpus luteum alive, so progesterone stays high and menstruation stops. hCG in urine is the basis of the **pregnancy test**.

**Terms:** amenorrhoea (absence of menses), dysmenorrhoea (painful menses), menorrhagia (heavy bleeding). Oral contraceptive pills (oestrogen + progestin) work by suppressing FSH and LH, so ovulation does not occur.

## 11.6 Fertilisation and pregnancy

- **Fertilisation:** fusion of a sperm and a secondary oocyte, normally in the **ampulla of the uterine tube** within about 24 hours of ovulation. Only one sperm enters; the oocyte then completes meiosis II and the nuclei fuse → **zygote** (2n = 46).
- **Cleavage:** the zygote divides as it moves down the tube → morula → **blastocyst** (reaches the uterus in about 4–5 days).
- **Implantation:** the blastocyst sinks into the endometrium about **day 6–7** after fertilisation.
- **Placenta:** formed from the embryo's chorion (chorionic villi) and the mother's endometrium; joined to the fetus by the **umbilical cord** (two arteries, one vein). Maternal and fetal blood do **not** mix.

**Functions of the placenta:** exchange of O2 and CO2 (respiration); supply of nutrients; removal of wastes; passage of maternal antibodies (IgG); barrier to many (not all) microbes and drugs; **endocrine** – hCG, oestrogen, progesterone, human placental lactogen. Some drugs cross the placenta and can harm the fetus (e.g. thalidomide, alcohol), so pharmacists must check drugs in pregnancy.

**Pregnancy (gestation):** about **40 weeks (280 days) from the first day of the last menstrual period**, divided into three trimesters. Embryo up to 8 weeks (organs form – most sensitive to drugs); fetus from 9 weeks to birth.

**Changes in the mother:** uterus enlarges; menstruation stops; breasts enlarge; increased blood volume, cardiac output and breathing; weight gain; nausea in early weeks; frequent urination.

**Membranes and fluid:** the **amnion** encloses the fetus in **amniotic fluid**, which cushions it and allows movement.

## 11.7 Parturition (childbirth)

**Parturition** is the birth of the baby at the end of pregnancy. The process of getting there is **labour**.

**Hormonal and nervous control**

1. Near term, oestrogen rises and progesterone's calming effect on the uterus falls; oxytocin receptors increase.
2. The fetus presses on the cervix → stretch → impulses to the hypothalamus → **oxytocin** released from the posterior pituitary.
3. Oxytocin (and prostaglandins) → stronger uterine contractions → more pressure on the cervix → more oxytocin.
4. This **positive feedback** loop continues until the baby is born.

```text
  Baby's head stretches cervix → nerve impulses → hypothalamus
        ↑                                              ↓
  Stronger contractions  ←  OXYTOCIN (posterior pituitary) + prostaglandins
        (cycle repeats until delivery – POSITIVE FEEDBACK)
```

**Stages of labour**

| Stage | What happens | Approx. duration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Dilation stage** | Regular contractions; cervix dilates fully to about 10 cm; amniotic sac ruptures ("waters break") | Longest – several hours (longer in a first baby) |
| **2. Expulsion stage** | Baby is pushed through the birth canal and delivered (usually head first) | Minutes to about 1–2 hours |
| **3. Placental stage** | Placenta (afterbirth) separates and is expelled; uterus contracts to stop bleeding | About 15–30 minutes |

**After birth:** **lactation** – prolactin (from the anterior pituitary) makes milk; oxytocin ejects it when the baby suckles. The first milk, **colostrum**, is rich in antibodies. Oxytocin-type drugs are used to start or strengthen labour and control bleeding after delivery.

## Remember

- Male: testes (sperm in seminiferous tubules, testosterone from Leydig cells) → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
- Seminal vesicles give fructose; prostate surrounds the urethra.
- Spermatogenesis: 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperm; oogenesis: 1 primary oocyte → 1 ovum + polar bodies.
- Female: ovaries, uterine tubes (fertilisation in ampulla), uterus (endometrium, myometrium, perimetrium), cervix, vagina.
- Menstrual cycle 28 days: menstrual (1–5), proliferative (FSH, oestrogen), ovulation (day 14, LH surge), secretory (progesterone from corpus luteum).
- hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive in pregnancy; it is detected by pregnancy tests.
- Pregnancy ≈ 40 weeks; placenta exchanges gases and nutrients and makes hormones.
- Parturition: oxytocin, positive feedback; three stages – dilation, expulsion, placental.
